name: libaegis (AEGIS-128L, AEGIS-128X/256X)
baseline: AES-256-GCM (SUPERCOP aes256gcmv1; on this host the fastest implementation is Romain Dolbeau's VAES code; the OpenSSL wrapper 'opensslnew' is also measured and is slower)
workload: eBACS/SUPERCOP AEAD 'long+0 encrypt' benchmark: cycles/byte for long messages with no associated data, computed as 1/1920 of the cycle-count difference between a 2048-byte and a 128-byte message (not 1536-byte messages)
claimed_speedup: long+0 encrypt quartiles on hertz: aegis128l 0.18/0.19/0.19 cycles/byte vs aes256gcmv1 0.55/0.56/0.57 cycles/byte, about 2.9-3x faster (derived from page data). 1536+1536 encrypt: aegis128l 0.20-0.21 vs aes256gcmv1 0.55-0.56. The wider AEGIS-128X4 variant (also in libaegis) measures 0.07-0.08 cycles/byte long+0, about 7-8x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: From the eBACS web-impl pages (SUPERCOP 20260831, hertz). Fastest aegis128l implementation 'aesnib': clang -march=native -O2 -fwrapv -Qunused-arguments -fPIC -fPIE -gdwarf-4 -Wall. Fastest aes256gcmv1 implementation 'dolbeau/vaesenc-int': clang -march=native -Os -fwrapv -Qunused-arguments -fPIC -fPIE -gdwarf-4 -Wall.
hardware: Intel Core i9-13900K (Raptor Lake); AMD EPYC 7543; AMD Ryzen 7 7700 (Zen4, AVX-512+VAES) — single core, 16 KB messages
stars_or_usage: 146 stars; AEGIS is now published as RFC 10032 (linked from the libaegis README) and is also shipped inside libsodium
tradeoffs: The X2/X4 speedups require VAES/AVX-512 or equivalent wide vector-AES instructions; on CPUs without vector-AES, plain AEGIS-128L/256 is as fast or faster than the X-variants. AEGIS has a shorter cryptanalytic track record than AES-GCM (in active study since 2013).
caveats: eBACS measures SUPERCOP's own AEGIS implementations, not libaegis. The winning aegis128l code on hertz is 'aesnib' (no author credited); Frank Denis's sodium-aesni (libsodium) scores close behind, and the aegis128x2/x4 code in SUPERCOP is credited to Frank Denis. The aes256gcmv1 row is the best of several AES-GCM implementations. On hertz that is dolbeau/vaesenc-int. The OpenSSL wrapper (opensslnew) is slower in the web-impl selection-time column: about 5764 for opensslnew vs 3258 for dolbeau and 1241 for aegis128l aesnib, so the gap against OpenSSL itself is likely larger than 3x. Compiler and flags ARE disclosed on the per-machine web-impl pages. libaegis's own README chart (img/bench-encryption.png, first-party, 16 KB encryption) does state its CPUs. On AMD Zen 4 with turbo off: aegis128l 208.44 Gb/s vs aes256-gcm (BoringSSL) 47.68 Gb/s. On Apple M1: 114.61 vs 41.6 Gb/s. The chart's baseline is BoringSSL, not OpenSSL, and the libaegis benchmark.zig does not include AES-GCM.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos aead cipher c++ (surfaced aegis-aead/libaegis); corroborated via bench.cr.yp.to/results-aead/amd64-hertz.html
IACR ePrint search q=AEGIS: https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/523 'Adding more parallelism to the AEGIS authenticated encryption algorithms'

verification.tier_reason: eBACS/SUPERCOP is a well-known independent suite. On the hertz page (Ryzen 7 7700) aegis128l runs at 0.18-0.19 cycles/byte and aes256gcmv1 at 0.55-0.57. The public harness and web-impl pages give compiler, flags and CPU, but the measured aegis128l code (the uncredited 'aesnib' implementation) is not shown to be libaegis. The fastest AES-GCM is also Dolbeau's VAES code, not OpenSSL, so this is B, not A.
verification.notes: The numbers are accurate and belong to the aegis128l and aes256gcmv1 rows. The workload wrongly said 1536-byte messages; 'long' is the 2048-vs-128-byte differential. The record's caveats wrongly said compiler flags were undisclosed and the README charts had no CPU, and both are corrected. Tier would be A for the AEGIS algorithm vs OpenSSL AES-GCM, but the measured code is not shown to be libaegis's.

name: chacha20poly1305-simd
workload: AEAD seal (encrypt_in_place_detached), 16-byte AAD, in-place, across message sizes from 16 B to ≥16 KiB
claimed_speedup: 2.0-3.1x faster than OpenSSL 4.1.0-dev at tiny sizes (16-256B), 1.3-1.9x at mid sizes (512B-1KiB), 1.0-1.1x at large sizes (>=4KiB); also 1.7-6.2x vs RustCrypto chacha20poly1305 0.11 (same ISA tier) and 0.8-1.4x vs aws-lc-rs depending on size
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.100-nightly; cargo bench --bench aead (Criterion; bench profile codegen-units=1; runtime SIMD dispatch, no target-cpu flag). OpenSSL 4.1.0-dev static build with runtime auto-dispatch (AVX-512 ChaCha and AVX-512 IFMA Poly1305 on this CPU). The OpenSSL driver perf/openssl_bench.c is built with cc -O2. aws-lc-rs 1.18 is benchmarked in the same Criterion harness.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (Zen 4), Linux
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (GitHub repo created 2026-08-26; crate first published 2026-08-27); 108 crates.io downloads (v0.3.1)
tradeoffs: Disclaimer in README: developed with AI assistance and has not undergone a security audit; pure Rust with hand-written AVX-512/AVX2/SSE2/NEON backends and runtime CPU dispatch
caveats: A very new project (Aug 2026) with no independent verification. The README says it was developed with AI assistance and has not had a security audit. The OpenSSL comparison uses an OpenSSL 4.1.0-dev pre-release, and the setups are asymmetric: the C driver calls EVP_EncryptInit_ex with the cipher and key on every iteration, while the Rust cipher is keyed once outside the loop. That likely inflates the 2-3x gap at 16-256 B. At >=64 KiB it merely ties OpenSSL. Against aws-lc-rs it is slower at tiny sizes (0.8-0.9x) and about even at 512 B-1 KiB. It wins only at >=4 KiB (1.2-1.4x).

name: hardware-rust-crypto
workload: AES-256-GCM allocation-free encrypt/decrypt (encrypt_to/decrypt_to), Criterion benchmarks over sizes 16B-16KiB
claimed_speedup: Allocation-free encrypt beats ring at every size from 16 B to 16 KiB: 26.8 vs 57.8 ns at 16 B, 130.5 vs 216.6 ns at 1 KiB, and 1.77 vs 2.38 us at 16 KiB (8.64 vs 6.41 GiB/s). Decrypt also wins: 1.79 vs 2.19 us at 16 KiB. Against a default-build RustCrypto aes-gcm 0.10 it is 14x-43x faster. Against RustCrypto with its ARMv8 cfgs it is 3.4x-5.0x faster at >=256 B, but only ~1.3x-1.7x at 16-64 B. ring's key setup is faster (86 vs 94 ns).
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.96.0, cargo bench (Criterion, default release build); RustCrypto 'armv8 cfgs' variant built with RUSTFLAGS="--cfg aes_armv8 --cfg polyval_armv8"
hardware: Apple M4 Max, macOS (Darwin 25.4)
tradeoffs: AES-256-only (no AES-128), hardware-instruction-only design (no software fallback, so it hard-fails on CPUs lacking AES-NI/ARMv8 crypto extensions); extensively formally verified (Kani, SAW, crux-mir, F*, Z3) as its other main selling point besides speed
caveats: This is a single-run laptop benchmark. The author states +/-10% run-to-run variance at sub-microsecond sizes and says to read results as 'tie/win/lose, not exact ratios' and to re-run on target Linux x86_64 hardware before integration decisions; no x86_64 numbers are published. The 14x-43x figure is against a RustCrypto build whose hardware AES is off by default on aarch64. It is not a GitHub fork, but per its NOTICE it vendors and adapts hasenbanck/rand_aes 0.7.0 (AES) and RustCrypto ghash/polyval backends. OpenSSL is used only for interop tests, not benchmarks. Only AES-256 is supported. The project has only 1 GitHub star.
found_via: crates.io API q=aes-ni, per-page=15

verification.notes: The numbers match docs/benchmarks.md. The record overstated the win over RustCrypto's ARMv8 build: 3.4-5.0x holds only from 256 B up. The main claim against ring (BoringSSL-derived) is accurate.

name: HiAE (High-throughput Authenticated Encryption)
workload: Single-core AEAD encrypt+authenticate throughput across 14 named ARM and x86 CPUs (server/desktop/laptop/mobile/router), message sizes 64B-16384B, -O3 builds, vs OpenSSL 3.0 AES-256-GCM, AES-256-CTR, SNOW-V-GCM, Rocca, Rocca-S and AEGIS-128L.
claimed_speedup: AEAD at 16384 B (Table 10): 340.02 Gbps (HiAE) vs 51.90 Gbps (OpenSSL 3.0 AES-256-GCM) on AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (~6.6x, derived from page data); 171.46 vs 36.49 Gbps on Intel Xeon W9-3495X (~4.7x, derived from page data); 253.19 vs 38.80 Gbps on AMD EPYC 9334 (~6.5x, derived from page data). The abstract states over 340 Gbps on x86 and 180 Gbps on ARM in AEAD mode, 'making it the fastest AEAD solution on ARM chips and setting a new performance record on the latest x86 processors'.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.4 (x86 servers/desktop, Ubuntu 22.04 or WSL2), GCC 10.3 (Kunpeng/openEuler), GCC 14 (Apple M-series), ArkCompiler 3.0.0.5 (Huawei mobile), openWRT GCC 11.2.0 (router); -O3 maximum optimization used for every implementation compared
hardware: 14 CPUs in Table 9/10: Intel Xeon W9-3495X, AMD EPYC 9334, AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, Intel Xeon Gold 6326, Intel Core i7-11700, Intel Xeon Gold 6242R, Intel Xeon E5-2620 v3, HiSilicon Kunpeng 920, Kunpeng 920X, Kirin 9000S, Qualcomm Snapdragon 8+ Gen1, Apple M2 Max, Apple M3 Pro, Rockchip RK3568 (an M1 MacBook Air is named in the setup text but has no result row)
tradeoffs: Reference repo carries no LICENSE file, so the code can be studied but not safely reused/redistributed as-is. HiAE is a brand-new (2025) design with far less cryptanalysis history than AES-GCM or even AEGIS; the paper's own results show HiAE falls slightly behind Rocca on older Xeon Gold 6242R/E5-2620 v3 CPUs that lack VAES.
caveats: Very new design (2025) by the paper's authors; numbers are first-party, from a non-peer-reviewed preprint. The public repo harness (test/performance_test.c) benchmarks HiAE only; the OpenSSL comparison code is not published. On mobile phones the AES-256 baseline was hand-implemented rather than OpenSSL. HiAE trails Rocca on pre-VAES Xeons (Gold 6242R, E5-2620 v3). Under active cryptanalysis: ePrint 2025/1180 'Cryptanalysis of the Authenticated Stream Cipher HiAE' (now a minor revision of a ToSC 2026 paper), 2025/1203 'Analyze the Security of the AEAD Scheme HiAE by Algebraic Techniques', and the designers' rebuttal 2025/1235. The reference repo has no license file; an MIT-licensed implementation exists at hiae-aead/libhiae (59 stars), but its README does not benchmark against AES-GCM.
found_via: IACR ePrint search q=HiAE: https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/377 'HiAE: A High-Throughput Authenticated Encryption Algorithm for Cross-Platform Efficiency'

verification.tier_reason: ePrint 2025/377 Table 10 does compare HiAE against OpenSSL 3.0 AES-256-GCM on 14 named CPUs with GCC version and -O3 stated, but the paper is a non-peer-reviewed preprint by the designers (ePrint lists 'Publication info: Preprint'; no venue found on Crossref), and the public harness (test/performance_test.c) times only HiAE with no OpenSSL/baseline code, so it is neither A (baseline benchmark code not public) nor B (not peer-reviewed/independent).
verification.notes: All three quoted numbers match Table 10 exactly; the only fix is marking the ratios as derived (7950X is 6.55x, not 6.5x). Metadata checked: no LICENSE file, not archived or a fork, 21 stars, last commit 2025-11-11 (active). Orchestrator may prefer hiae-aead/libhiae (MIT) as the copyable repo, but that is a different project URL, so I did not change repo_url.

name: HiAE (libhiae)
workload: AEAD encryption with associated data and tag, 64 KB messages, 4096-byte-aligned buffers
claimed_speedup: On Apple M5 Max with 64 KB messages, HiAE (a vendored libhiae copy) reaches 266.7 Gbps AEAD encryption against 70.8 Gbps for OpenSSL 3.6.4 AES-128-GCM (~3.77x, derived from page data). Separately, the designers' ePrint 2025/377 paper benchmarks their own Concyclics/HiAE implementation, not libhiae, against OpenSSL 3.0. Its abstract claims over 340 Gbps (x86) and 180 Gbps (ARM) for AEAD. Table 10, AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, 16384-byte messages: AEAD 340.02 Gbps vs AES-256-GCM 51.90 Gbps (~6.6x, derived from paper data); encryption-only 352.73 Gbps vs AES-256-CTR 95.71 Gbps (~3.7x, derived). The record's 269.01 vs 84.09 Gbps pair is encryption-only at 1024 bytes against AES-256-CTR, not AEAD against AES-256-GCM.
compiler_and_flags: M5 Max run: Apple clang 21.0.0 on macOS 26, -O3 -mcpu=native, OpenSSL 3.6.4. Paper: GCC 11.4 -O3 on the x86 servers (Ubuntu 22.04) and on the desktop (Windows 11 WSL2, Ubuntu 22.04, which includes the 7950X), and GCC 14 on the Apple laptops.
hardware: Apple M5 Max (macOS 26) for the AES-GCM comparison. The page also has a Zen 4 (Ryzen 7 7700, 3.8 GHz fixed) run, but its text table gives no AES-GCM figure. The paper covers 14 CPUs (Table 9), including the AMD Ryzen 9 7950X and Intel Xeon W9-3495X.
tradeoffs: Newer, non-standardized AES-based AEAD tied to an individual IETF CFRG draft (draft-pham-cfrg-hiae) and ePrint 2025/377; best performance needs clang/zig cc rather than gcc; HiAEx2/HiAEx4 variants are explicitly experimental benchmarking-only, not part of the spec
caveats: The benchmark repo (hiae-aead/benchmarks, no LICENSE file) is maintained by libhiae's main author (jedisct1), so these are first-party measurements of a vendored libhiae copy. The ePrint 2025/377 figures measure a different implementation, the designers' Concyclics/HiAE (no license). The paper is still an ePrint preprint (4 revisions, last 2025-06-04) and no Crossref record for it was found. It accompanies draft-pham-cfrg-hiae (rev 06), which is an individual draft and not yet an RFC.

name: ROCCA-S
workload: AEAD encryption and decryption throughput at 64 KB messages, with 48-byte associated data plus the tag, sweeping sizes from 16 B to 64 KB. A separate keystream-only mode is compared against OpenSSL AES-128-CTR. Buffers are 4096-byte aligned. Measured on Apple M5 Max and AMD Ryzen 7 7700 (Zen 4).
claimed_speedup: At 64 KB on Apple M5 Max, ROCCA-S AEAD runs at 208.1 Gbps encryption and 140.4 Gbps decryption, against OpenSSL AES-128-GCM's 70.8 and 70.2 Gbps (~2.9x encryption, ~2.0x decryption, derived from page data). Its keystream path runs at 228.8 Gbps against OpenSSL AES-128-CTR's 159.6 (~1.4x, derived from page data). On Zen 4 (Ryzen 7 7700 locked at 3.8 GHz), ROCCA-S does 174.6 Gbps encryption and 92.3 Gbps decryption, against AES-128-GCM's 92.7 and 92.9 Gbps. That is ~1.9x on encryption, but decryption is at parity, about 0.99x (derived from page data; the Zen 4 GCM figures appear only in the README's bar chart).
compiler_and_flags: M5: Apple clang 21.0.0, -O3 -mcpu=native (the Makefile uses -mcpu=native on arm64), with OpenSSL 3.6.4. Zen 4: clang 21.1.8, -O3 -march=native, with OpenSSL 3.5.5. All builds also use -std=c99.
hardware: Apple Silicon M5 Max (macOS 26); AMD Ryzen 7 7700 (Zen 4) at fixed 3.8GHz, performance governor, boost disabled
stars_or_usage: 2 stars. KDDI's official reference implementation of Rocca-S (ESORICS 2023: 'An Ultra-High Throughput AES-based Authenticated Encryption Scheme for 6G'). The spec is IETF individual draft draft-nakano-rocca-s-06 (2026-01-28). It was presented at CFRG IETF-115, was never adopted, and expired on 2026-08-01.
tradeoffs: 256-bit key / 256-bit tag only; decryption is 1.5-1.9x slower than encryption at large message sizes because the AES-round-then-fold state update recovers the message block only after the AES round completes; needs AES-NI or ARM crypto extensions to hit peak throughput
caveats: The comparison numbers come from a separate repo, hiae-aead/benchmarks. It lives under the HiAE org, almost all commits are by jedisct1, and it has no top-level license. Its rocca-s/rocca-s.c is a reformatted copy of KDDI's MIT reference with an added ARM-crypto (vaeseq/vaesmcq) backend, so the M5 figures measure that port, not yt-nakano's code as-is; yt-nakano's code supports only x86 AES-NI plus a portable table fallback. The yt-nakano README itself gives only a standalone '>200 Gbps on i9-12900K' figure with no baseline. The comparison is 256-bit-key Rocca-S against AES-128-GCM, not the like-for-like AES-256-GCM. Decryption is much slower than encryption (1.48x slower on M5, 1.89x on Zen 4), and on Zen 4 decryption only matches OpenSSL's VAES GCM. On security, Rocca-S is not key-committing. Practical FROB committing attacks with a test vector are in Takeuchi-Todo-Iwata, ePrint 2024/901, which extends their ToSC 2024(2) attack on revised Rocca and improves Derbez et al., ToSC 2024(1), which needed 2^64. The same note found an equivalent-key issue in the short-key expansion, fixed in draft-06; the reference code takes 256-bit keys only. The ToSC 2024(2) key-recovery and universal-forgery results target Rocca-v2/v3/v4, not Rocca-S; the paper notes that Rocca-S shares v4's unkeyed finalization and leaves Rocca-S open. I found no published key-recovery or nonce-respecting forgery against Rocca-S.
found_via: GitHub: search 'AEAD in:readme benchmark AES-NI' surfaced hiae-aead/benchmarks; canonical repo found via search 'rocca-s' -> yt-nakano/rocca-s

corrected_fields.caveats: The comparison numbers come from a separate repo (hiae-aead/benchmarks), maintained by the HiAE algorithm's authors rather than an independent third party, though it states full compiler/flags/CPU/OpenSSL-version methodology and ships runnable build+benchmark scripts, which is why it still qualifies for tier A. The canonical yt-nakano/rocca-s README itself only gives a standalone '>200 Gbps on i9-12900K' figure with no baseline comparison.

name: SNOW-V-GCM
workload: Single-thread AEAD encryption throughput vs input size (64B-16384B) on a laptop CPU; SNOW-V-GCM implemented in C++ with AVX2/AES-NI/PCLMULQDQ intrinsics, benchmarked using code extracted from OpenSSL's own benchmarking harness against OpenSSL 3.0.0-dev (2019-04-01) AES-256-GCM assembly.
claimed_speedup: Table 3, AEAD, 16384 B: 38.91 Gbps (SNOW-V-GCM C++) vs 34.42 Gbps (OpenSSL AES-256-GCM asm), ~13% faster (derived from page data). Roughly even at 2048 B (30.71 vs 30.49); AES-256-GCM wins at 1024 B and below (e.g. 64 B: 8.54 vs 5.16 Gbps).
compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2017 + NASM, 'most possible optimizations switched on', native x64 build
hardware: Intel Core i7-8650U @1.90GHz (Turbo up to 4.20GHz), single thread
stars_or_usage: SNOW-V is a 3GPP/ETSI candidate stream cipher for 5G; no widely used, independently maintained open-source repo of SNOW-V-GCM was located in this search
tradeoffs: Only faster than OpenSSL AES-256-GCM for larger messages (roughly >=4KB); for short messages (<2KB) OpenSSL's hand-tuned, instruction-stitched assembly wins outright. The paper's own C++ implementation does not get GHASH "for free" the way OpenSSL's asm does.
caveats: Single 2018-era ultrabook CPU against a pre-release OpenSSL snapshot (3.0.0-dev, 2019-04-01); the win is small (~13%) and only above ~2 KB. The paper prints the SNOW-V AVX2 keystream code and a portable SNOW-V-GCM reference, but not the PCLMULQDQ-optimized GCM build or the harness that produced Table 3. Counter-evidence: HiAE (ePrint 2025/377, Table 10) measured the official SNOW-V-GCM implementation well below OpenSSL 3.0 AES-256-GCM on every modern x86 CPU tested (e.g. 19.92 vs 51.90 Gbps on Ryzen 9 7950X, 13.04 vs 36.49 Gbps on Xeon W9-3495X at 16 KB). No maintained public repo, so usability is 'reference'.
found_via: IACR ePrint search q=SNOW-V: https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/1143 'A new SNOW stream cipher called SNOW-V'

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed paper (ePrint 2018/1143, published by the IACR in FSE 2020). Table 3 shows SNOW-V-GCM beating OpenSSL 3.0.0-dev AES-256-GCM asm at 16 KB on a named i7-8650U. It falls short of A: compiler flags are only 'most possible optimizations switched on', the benchmark harness adapted from OpenSSL is not published, and the benchmarked AVX2/PCLMULQDQ SNOW-V-GCM build is not printed (Appendix D has a portable GHASH reference, and Appendix E has AVX2 code only for the SNOW-V keystream).
verification.notes: Numbers and setup (VS2017 + NASM, i7-8650U, single thread) match the paper exactly. The tier drops from A to B because neither the flags nor the benchmarked code/harness are public. Consider flagging this entry, because a later third-party measurement (the HiAE paper) contradicts the speed win on current CPUs.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: 16384B: 38.91 Gbps (SNOW-V-GCM) vs 34.42 Gbps (AES-256-GCM asm), ~13% faster. Advantage shrinks with message size and reverses below ~2048B (e.g. at 64B, AES-256-GCM wins: 8.54 Gbps vs 5.16 Gbps).
corrected_fields.caveats: Benchmarked on a single, now-old (2018-era) ultrabook CPU against a pre-release OpenSSL snapshot (3.0.0-dev); no maintained public repo found, so usability is 'reference' rather than 'copyable' even though full source is printed in the paper's appendix.

name: AEZ (v4)
workload: long+long encrypt, AES-NI implementation crypto_aead/aezv4/aesni, cycles/byte on a real CPU via the eBACS/SUPERCOP harness. 'long' is SUPERCOP's differential rate: 1/1920 of the cycle difference between a 2048-byte and a 128-byte message (here with the same length of associated data).
claimed_speedup: ~2.7x lower cycles/byte than aes256gcmv1 (0.26 vs 0.70 median, long+long encrypt); decrypt ~2.2x (0.26 vs 0.57); range across the page's 15 sections 1.9x (0+long) to 6.9x (64+64 forgery, noisy row) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: aezv4/aesni fastest with clang -march=native -O -fwrapv -Qunused-arguments -fPIC -fPIE -gdwarf-4 -Wall (Debian Clang 19.1.7). The other clang/gcc -O2/-O3/-Os builds are within 1%. Baseline aes256gcmv1: fastest implementation dolbeau/aesenc-int, clang -march=native -O2 -fwrapv -Qunused-arguments -fPIC -fPIE -gdwarf-4 -Wall (Debian Clang 19.1.7); dolbeau/vaesenc-int is within 4%, and SUPERCOP's OpenSSL wrapper (opensslnew, gcc -O2) is 1.46x slower.
hardware: amd64, Raptor Cove P-cores, 2024 Intel Core 5 210H, 4 x 2200MHz (eBACS machine "freshwrap,big")
stars_or_usage: 104 stars (floodyberry/supercop mirror); still included in current eBACS/SUPERCOP releases
tradeoffs: Non-standard, misuse-resistant (nonce-reuse-resistant) AEAD with variable-length tags/nonces, wide-block-cipher design (AEZ) rather than a stream+MAC AEAD; not adopted in any mainstream TLS/library stack; the design underwent several security revisions (v1-v5) after cryptanalytic findings, and this repo only mirrors v3/v4 (not the latest v5).
caveats: Public-domain dedication in the Unlicense wording (Ted Krovetz, 'free and unencumbered software'), so no patent grant. The baseline is SUPERCOP's fastest AES-256-GCM (Romain Dolbeau's AES-NI intrinsics), which beats SUPERCOP's OpenSSL wrapper, so the comparison is against a strong AES-GCM. The mirror is a stale 2016 snapshot, and the numbers come from the live bench.cr.yp.to page (supercop-20260627 dataset). eBACS results tables do not label which implementation or compiler produced each row. The aesni/compiler attribution comes from the web-impl pages. AEZ v4 was superseded by v5 (CAESAR round 3), which has about the same speed on this page (0.28).
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "AEZ" "authenticated encryption" -> floodyberry/supercop:crypto_aead/aezv4; cross-checked against eBACS AEAD results page

verification.tier_reason: Upgraded B->A. The independent eBACS/SUPERCOP harness is public (supercop-20260627 crypto_aead/measure.c, running crypto_aead/aezv4/aesni, which is in the linked mirror) and measures aes256gcmv1 on the same machine. The web-impl pages give the compiler and flags for every implementation (aezv4/aesni: clang 19.1.7 -march=native -O ...), and the results page gives the CPU (Intel Core 5 210H, Raptor Cove).
verification.notes: The numbers match the aezv4 and aes256gcmv1 rows of the long+long encrypt table exactly (0.26/0.26/0.27 and 0.69/0.70/0.71). The record's claim that no compiler was stated was wrong: the linked web-impl pages list per-implementation compilers and flags. Metadata checks out: 104 stars, no repo license, not a fork, last commit 2016-07-16, and the aesni/encrypt.c header is Unlicense text.

name: Bitsliced AEGIS-128L / AEGIS-128X2 (constant-time, no-AES-NI platforms)
workload: Single-core, 16 KB message AEAD encrypt+authenticate throughput on ARM/RISC-V CPUs lacking AES instructions and on WebAssembly, plus ARM Cortex-M4 cycle counts, vs side-channel-protected (bitsliced) AES-128-GCM from OpenSSL 3.3 (on Cortex-A53) and BoringSSL (elsewhere); also a pure-TypeScript benchmark on Apple M5 Max/Bun vs the noble-ciphers pure-JS AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305.
claimed_speedup: Paper Table 2, 16 KB messages, vs side-channel-protected (bitsliced) AES-128-GCM: ARM Cortex-A53 423 Mb/s (AEGIS-128L) vs 261 Mb/s (OpenSSL 3.3), 1.6x; SpacemiT X60 RISC-V 193 (128L) / 333 (128X2) vs 137 Mb/s (BoringSSL), 1.4-2.4x; SiFive U74 182 / 311 vs 130 Mb/s, 1.4-2.4x; WebAssembly on an Apple M1 host 2241 / 2912 vs 480 Mb/s, 4.7-6.1x. Cortex-M4: 185 cycles/byte (bitsliced AEGIS-128L) vs 246 (fixsliced AES-128-GCM, protected GHASH) and 208 (unprotected table AES-128-GCM). Table 3, pure TypeScript on Apple M5 Max/Bun, 1 MB: 324 MB/s (AEGIS-128L) vs 182 MB/s (noble AES-128-GCM, 1.8x) and 256 MB/s (noble ChaCha20-Poly1305, 1.3x).
hardware: ARM Cortex-A53 (64-bit); SpacemiT X60 (RISC-V, no AES ext.); SiFive U74 (RISC-V, no AES ext.); WebAssembly on an Apple M1 host; ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller; Apple M5 Max (pure TypeScript under Bun)
stars_or_usage: 9 stars (aegis-aead/aegis-bitsliced); companion pure-TypeScript port jedisct1/js-aegis-aead (MIT, 4 stars) used for the JS numbers
tradeoffs: Purpose-built for platforms lacking AES/vector-AES instructions (microcontrollers, RISC-V without crypto extensions, WASM, plain JS). On hardware with AES-NI/VAES, hardware-accelerated AEGIS or the AEGIS-X modes (see separate entry) are faster than this bitsliced code.
caveats: Published 2026-06/07 as a non-peer-reviewed preprint by the implementation's author; not yet independently reproduced. The C/Zig benchmark harness (src/test/benchmark.zig) measures only AEGIS variants; the baseline AES-GCM runs are not part of the published code, and compilers/flags are unstated. The repo README currently shows different, higher WebAssembly figures (AEGIS-128X2 3154, AEGIS-128L 3429 Mb/s) than the paper (2912 / 2241 Mb/s). The JS comparison uses the companion repo jedisct1/js-aegis-aead, whose 'bun run bench' does include noble-ciphers, but that baseline is not the listed OpenSSL/BoringSSL one.
found_via: IACR ePrint search q=AEGIS: https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1338 'Bitslicing the AEGIS'

verification.tier_reason: ePrint 2026/1338 ('Bitslicing the AEGIS', Frank Denis) is a preprint by the repo author, not a peer-reviewed paper, so the evidence is first-party and B does not apply. It is not A either: the public harness (src/test/benchmark.zig) times only AEGIS, not the OpenSSL/BoringSSL AES-GCM baselines, and compiler/flags are unstated.
verification.notes: All claimed numbers appear in the paper, but the X60 figure (333 Mb/s) is AEGIS-128X2, not 128L, so I labeled the variants. GitHub reports license NOASSERTION; the LICENSE file is plain MIT (Frank Denis, based on Adomnicai's work). Repo: 9 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-21 (active). ePrint lists the paper as CC0, but the code is MIT.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: ARM Cortex-A53: 423 Mb/s (AEGIS-128L) vs 261 Mb/s (protected AES-GCM), ~1.6x; WebAssembly on Apple M1 host: 2912 Mb/s (AEGIS-128X2) vs 480 Mb/s (protected AES-GCM), ~6.1x; SpacemiT X60 RISC-V: 333 Mb/s vs 137 Mb/s, ~2.4x; Cortex-M4: 185 cycles/byte (bitsliced AEGIS-128L) vs 246 c/B protected / 208 c/B unprotected AES-128-GCM; pure-JS on Apple M5 Max at 1 MB: 324 MB/s (AEGIS-128L) vs 182 MB/s (AES-128-GCM, ~1.8x) and 256 MB/s (ChaCha20-Poly1305, ~1.3x)
corrected_fields.caveats: Published 2026-09, very recent and not yet independently reproduced outside the authors' own two repos. The paper states baselines were 'built and run on the same machines' but does not spell out exact compiler/flags for those builds, so this is capped at Tier B rather than A despite naming every CPU and publishing all code.

name: LeMac
baseline: AES-GCM in associated-data-only mode (GHASH/GMAC-style authentication), using Romain Dolbeau's public-domain AES-NI/PCLMUL implementation (benchmark/GCM/aesenc-int.c, from SUPERCOP), not OpenSSL
workload: MAC throughput in cycles/byte on 1 kB, 16 kB and 256 kB messages. Each MAC runs 1000 times over the same in-cache random message, and the most frequent rdpmc cycle count is reported. The AEADs (GCM, Rocca, Rocca-S, AEGIS, Tiaoxin) are run in associated-data-only mode.
claimed_speedup: LeMac 0.068 cycles/byte vs 0.286 cycles/byte for GCM (AD only) on 256 kB messages on Intel Ice Lake Xeon Gold 5320 (~4.2x, derived from page data). Other CPUs: Zen3 EPYC 7513 0.072 vs 0.451 (~6.3x, derived); Skylake Xeon Gold 6130 0.126 vs 0.370 (~2.9x, derived); Haswell Xeon E5-2630 v3 0.131 vs 0.605 (~4.6x, derived). The abstract's '60% throughput improvement' is measured against the Jean-Nikolic rate-2 MAC (0.113 cycles/byte on Ice Lake), the fastest prior MAC in the authors' benchmarks, not against GCM.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 12.2.0 (paper Section 7.2); -Wall -Wextra -O3 -march=native (benchmark/LeMac/Makefile, shared by benchmark/GCM)
hardware: Intel Ice Lake Xeon Gold 5320 (headline); also Intel Haswell Xeon E5-2630 v3, Intel Skylake Xeon Gold 6130, AMD Zen1 EPYC 7301, AMD Zen3 EPYC 7513
stars_or_usage: 2 stars (reference implementation repo); algorithm published IACR Trans. Symmetric Cryptol. (ToSC) 2024/2
tradeoffs: LeMac is a MAC/universal-hash primitive, not a complete AEAD; it must be paired with a stream cipher (e.g. AES-CTR) to form a full AES-GCM replacement, so it cannot be dropped in on its own; a sibling construction (LeMac-0) had a message-schedule bug in the original paper, fixed in this repo; CC0-1.0 dedication carries no patent grant
caveats: The baseline is a public-domain SUPERCOP AES-GCM (Dolbeau aesenc-int.c) run in AD-only mode, not OpenSSL's GHASH, and LeMac is a MAC only (no encryption). The paper benchmarked LeMac-0, whose specification erratum was later fixed and renamed; the README says performance is unaffected. The repo, with its benchmark code, was first committed on 2024-09-13, after the paper's 2024-06-18 publication, and ships no result files. Code is CC0 plus an MIT-licensed bundled AES from boppreh/aes, with no patent grant under CC0.
found_via: SUPERCOP eBACS AEAD benchmark fastest implementations -> found via 'Rocca: reference code from the ePrint paper' cross-reference inside AugustinBariant/Implementations_LeMac_PetitMac benchmark README -> IACR ToSC article 11619

verification.tier_reason: Upgraded from B to A. The paper's Table 4 (ToSC 2024/2, peer-reviewed) benchmarks LeMac directly against GCM in associated-data-only mode on named CPUs (Xeon Gold 5320 Ice Lake and others) and states gcc 12.2.0. The benchmark code is public in this repo (benchmark/benchmarks script, benchmark/LeMac/bench.c, benchmark/GCM/bench.c), with -O3 -march=native set in benchmark/LeMac/Makefile, which benchmark/GCM uses as well.
verification.notes: The abstract figures (0.068 c/B on Ice Lake, a 60% improvement) are correct, but the 60% is relative to the Jean-Nikolic MAC; the GCM comparison is in Table 4 of the PDF. All parts carry OSI or CC0 licenses, so usability is copyable rather than mixed. The last commit is 2025-07-10 (stale), and the benchmarks for HiAE, EliMAC and aegis128x2 were added in 2025 with no published results.

name: MORUS-1280
workload: eBACS/SUPERCOP harness on a real CPU, AVX2 implementation crypto_aead/morus1280256v1/avx2, cycles/byte for all 15 sections of the page. 'long' is SUPERCOP's differential rate: 1/1920 of the cycle difference between a 2048-byte and a 128-byte message (here with the same length of associated data).
claimed_speedup: Mixed, workload-dependent (derived from page data): faster than aes256gcmv1 on long+0 (1.55x encrypt, 0.69 vs 1.07; 1.19x decrypt, 0.68 vs 0.81), long+long encrypt (1.06x, 0.66 vs 0.70) and 64+64 (1.11-1.18x). Slower on long+long decrypt/forgery (0.67 vs 0.57, ~0.85x), 1536+1536 decrypt (0.82 vs 0.70) and 0+long AD-only (0.65 vs 0.32-0.33, ~0.5x).
compiler_and_flags: morus1280256v1/avx2 fastest with clang -march=native -O3 -fwrapv -Qunused-arguments -fPIC -fPIE -gdwarf-4 -Wall (Debian Clang 19.1.7). Baseline aes256gcmv1: fastest implementation dolbeau/aesenc-int, clang -march=native -O2 -fwrapv -Qunused-arguments -fPIC -fPIE -gdwarf-4 -Wall (Debian Clang 19.1.7); dolbeau/vaesenc-int is within 4%, and SUPERCOP's OpenSSL wrapper (opensslnew, gcc -O2) is 1.46x slower.
hardware: amd64, Raptor Cove P-cores, 2024 Intel Core 5 210H, 4 x 2200MHz (eBACS machine "freshwrap,big")
stars_or_usage: 104 stars (floodyberry/supercop mirror); still included in current eBACS/SUPERCOP releases
tradeoffs: Margin over AES-GCM is small (~6%) on this AES-NI-equipped CPU and within measurement noise on some other machines/sections of the same page; not standardized, not adopted in production stacks; ARX/AES-round hybrid CAESAR finalist.
caveats: The claimed win is marginal and one-directional on this Raptor Cove machine. MORUS is faster than SUPERCOP's fastest AES-256-GCM on encrypt and message-only workloads (up to 1.55x on long+0 encrypt). It is about 15% slower on long+long and 1536+1536 decrypt/forgery and about 2x slower when only associated data is authenticated. The record's earlier caveat that the gap 'narrows further' on other sections was wrong, because the gap reverses. No license header in the avx2 source (CAESAR-era submission, terms unclear), so reference/study use only. The baseline is Dolbeau's AES-NI AES-GCM, not OpenSSL, and the mirror is a stale 2016 snapshot.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos/code for MORUS CAESAR AEAD implementations -> floodyberry/supercop:crypto_aead/morus1280256v1; cross-checked against eBACS AEAD results page

Decrypt and AD-heavy sections show MORUS slower than AES-256-GCM. reject:not-faster is arguable, but it keeps a real (up to 1.55x) win on message-only encrypt. Metadata is correct: no license in morus1280256v1avx2.c, last commit 2016-07-16, 104 stars.

name: Rocca (AES-based AEAD for 6G)
workload: Single-thread throughput in encryption-only and AEAD modes, messages 64B to 16384B, 13-byte associated data. AEAD mode repeats init, AD, encryption, tag and finalization for every message. Rocca, SNOW-V, Tiaoxin-346 and AEGIS (from SUPERCOP) were built into OpenSSL (latest PDF says 3.1.0-dev; the Jan 2022 revision says 3.0.0-alpha3-Dev) and compared with OpenSSL's AES-256-GCM/CTR/CBC, ChaCha20 and ChaCha20-Poly1305, and SNOW-V-GCM.
claimed_speedup: 16384B AEAD on i7-1068NG7 (Table 7): Rocca 150.95 Gbps vs OpenSSL AES-256-GCM 29.08 Gbps (~5.2x, derived from page data) and vs ChaCha20-Poly1305 7.60 Gbps (~19.9x, derived from page data). The paper text says 4.16x faster than SNOW-V and 3.10x faster than AES-256-CTR at 16384B; both figures come from the encryption-only rows. The lead shrinks on other CPUs and for small messages. On the i9-11900 (Appendix A, Table 9), 16384B AEAD is 175.12 vs AES-256-GCM 117.60 Gbps (~1.5x, derived from page data), and Rocca is slower than AES-256-GCM at 256B (13.81 vs 15.57 Gbps) and at 64B (3.68 vs 4.51 Gbps). These numbers are for the revised Rocca (key feedforward in initialization). The original peer-reviewed ToSC 2021 paper reports 138.22 Gbps vs AES-256-GCM 30.59 and ChaCha20-Poly1305 7.57 Gbps at 16384B AEAD.
hardware: Main table (Table 7): Intel Core i7-1068NG7 @2.30GHz, 32GB RAM. Appendix A adds Intel i9-12900K, i9-11900 and i9-10910 (Windows 10 Pro / macOS Big Sur 11.4), plus ARM NEON builds on Apple M1, Apple A15 Bionic and Qualcomm Snapdragon 888.
license: CC BY (license of the ePrint 2022/116 paper; the reference implementation exists only in the paper's Appendix C)
stars_or_usage: Peer-reviewed in IACR ToSC 2021(2) (presented at FSE 2022). ePrint 2022/116 is the full version: 4 revisions, last on 2023-03-16. The only standalone code found is a third-party C implementation of the original Rocca, ericlagergren/rocca (BSD-3-Clause, 5 stars, last commit 2022-01-28, no benchmarks). The successor Rocca-S has separate implementations such as jedisct1/zig-rocca-s (MIT, 21 stars).
tradeoffs: The original Rocca was later shown to have practical forgery/committing weaknesses (see IACR ePrint 2024/901 and the ToSC 2024/2025 Derbez et al. and Takeuchi et al. papers) and was superseded by the redesigned Rocca-S. Treat these numbers as a data point on the AES-NI+SIMD 'wide round function' technique, not as a currently-recommended cipher.
caveats: The numbers at benchmark_url (the latest ePrint PDF, 2023-03-16) are for the REVISED Rocca, which adds key feedforward in initialization after the Hosoyamada et al. ToSC 2022(3) attack: a full 256-bit key recovery with about 2^128 data and time, which breaks the original 256-bit claim. They are not for the original design. The original design's peer-reviewed numbers are in ToSC 2021(2): 138.22 vs 30.59 / 7.57 Gbps. Across ePrint revisions the OpenSSL baseline numbers stay identical to two decimals (AES-256-GCM 29.08 and ChaCha20-Poly1305 7.60 Gbps on the i7; 57.87 and 21.99 on the i9-12900K) while the OpenSSL version label and the Rocca numbers change. So the baselines were probably not re-measured. Compiler and flags are never stated. The advantage depends heavily on the CPU: only about 1.5x over AES-256-GCM on the i9-11900, and Rocca loses at 64B and 256B there. The code is C with AES-NI/NEON intrinsics, not C++. The design has since been superseded by Rocca-S.
found_via: IACR ePrint search q=Rocca AES-based encryption beyond 5G: https://eprint.iacr.org/2022/116 'Rocca: An Efficient AES-based Encryption Scheme for Beyond 5G (Full version)'

verification.tier_reason: Table 7 of ePrint 2022/116 compares Rocca, built into OpenSSL, with OpenSSL AES-256-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 on a named CPU (i7-1068NG7). ePrint 2022/116 is the full version and a major revision of the peer-reviewed ToSC 2021(2) paper, and that paper shows the same win (138.22 vs 30.59 Gbps). Tier A is impossible: the benchmark harness is not public and neither version states a compiler or flags. The only code is the reference C in Appendix C.
verification.notes: The record's name says 'original/pre-attack', but the numbers it cites (150.95 Gbps, OpenSSL 3.1.0-dev) belong to the revised Rocca in the 2023 ePrint revision. Either rename the entry to 'Rocca (revised, key feedforward)' or repoint benchmark_url to the ToSC 2021 paper (https://tosc.iacr.org/index.php/ToSC/article/download/8904/8480) and use its original-design numbers. The record's language field says C++, but the code is C. repo_url could point to ericlagergren/rocca (original Rocca, BSD-3-Clause), but that repo has no benchmarks.

name: Tiaoxin-346

claimed_speedup: ~4.7x lower cycles/byte than aes256gcmv1 (0.15 vs 0.70 median, long+long encrypt), but only ~2.0x on long+long decrypt/forgery (0.28 vs 0.57); range across the page's 15 sections 1.8x (long+0 decrypt) to 5.6x (long+0 encrypt, noisy row) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: tiaoxinv2/nim fastest with gcc -march=native -mtune=native -O2 -fwrapv -fPIC -fPIE -gdwarf-4 -Wall (gcc 14.2.0). Clang builds are 4-10% slower, and one clang configuration fails to compile (missing ssse3/aes target features). Baseline aes256gcmv1: fastest implementation dolbeau/aesenc-int, clang -march=native -O2 -fwrapv -Qunused-arguments -fPIC -fPIE -gdwarf-4 -Wall (Debian Clang 19.1.7); dolbeau/vaesenc-int is within 4%, and SUPERCOP's OpenSSL wrapper (opensslnew, gcc -O2) is 1.46x slower.

name: LeMac (pauldreik C++20 port)
workload: Single-core bulk MAC/digest throughput: LeMac oneshot() hashing 256 KB/1 MB buffers vs `openssl speed -evp SHA1`, same AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D machine (Debian 13 Trixie)
claimed_speedup: LeMac oneshot 76.7 GiB/s (256 kB) and 74.3 GiB/s (1 MB), median of 5 runs, vs about 2.8 GiB/s for OpenSSL SHA1 (`openssl speed -evp SHA1`) on the same AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D, i.e. ~26-27x (derived from page data). The same README also reports: xxh3/xxh128 reach about 89 GiB/s with `xxhsum -b`, 'about 16% faster than lemac' (LeMac does not beat xxh3); clhash reaches 0.11 cycles/byte vs LeMac's 0.067 cycles/byte, which the README states as clhash being 'about 39% slower than lemac' (equivalently LeMac ~1.6x clhash throughput, derived from page data); raw AES-128-ECB (`openssl speed -evp AES-128-ECB`) reaches about 16.4 GiB/s. On a Raspberry Pi 5, LeMac does about 11.4 GiB/s against 13.2 GiB/s for xxh and 3.4 GiB/s for AES-128-ECB.
compiler_and_flags: cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, with per-file flags from CMakeLists.txt on gcc/clang: -maes -msse2 for the AES-NI-128 path, and -maes -mvaes -mavx512f -mavx512vl for the VAES/AVX-512 path. The compiler is not named for the Zen4/Linux run (the README says Linux support is clang>=16 and gcc>=12); 'compiler: clang' is printed only for the Apple M3/M4 runs.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D, Debian 13 Trixie (primary bulk numbers, 77 GiB/s / 0.067 cycles/byte); also Apple M4 MacBook Air (48 GiB/s), Apple M3 MacBook Air, and Raspberry Pi 5 / Ubuntu 24.04 (11 GiB/s, thermally throttled per README)
tradeoffs: Requires AES-NI (amd64) or ARMv8 crypto extensions (arm64); no portable/software fallback yet (planned); ships a lemacsum CLI (sha256sum/xxhsum-style) plus a library API with reusable hasher objects to amortize ~5 KB init / ~2 KB finalize overhead; requires C++20.
caveats: The README compares only against SHA1 (OpenSSL EVP), raw AES-128-ECB (OpenSSL), xxh3/xxh128 (xxhsum -b) and clhash. It has no comparison against a MAC incumbent such as GMAC/GHASH, Poly1305, HMAC or AEGIS. LeMac is a nonce-based MAC, so beating SHA1 (a bare digest) is not a like-for-like comparison and is best read as directional evidence of AES-NI-class speed. LeMac loses to xxh3 on Zen4 and to xxh on the Pi 5. The compiler is not named for the primary Zen4 run, and the baseline numbers come from outside tools rather than the repo's benchmark. This port implements the corrected LeMac from the ToSC 2025(1) corrigendum (DOI 10.46586/tosc.v2025.i1.623-628), not LeMac-0. src/lemac_aesni_impl.h and src/lemac_arm64_v8A.cpp use the extra RR message-schedule register and 'Four final rounds', as in upstream commit d035564f 'Fix LeMac specification, and rename erroneous version as LeMac-0' (Oct 2024). test/tests.cpp asserts the corrected 'LeMac' test vectors (for example 52282e853c9cfeb5537d33fb916a341f for the empty message) rather than the LeMac-0 ones. Arm64 on Windows has no runtime check for hardware support.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/pauldreik/lemac (README.md Performance section, include/lemac.h, commit history)

verification.tier_reason: The README's 'Results on AMD zen4' section gives first-party numbers on a Ryzen 9 7950X3D: LeMac oneshot at 76.7 GiB/s (256 kB) and 74.3 GiB/s (1 MB), against SHA1 at about 2.8 GiB/s from `openssl speed -evp SHA1` on the same machine. The benchmark code is public (benchmark/benchmark.cpp) and flags can be read from CMakeLists.txt, but the compiler is not named for the Zen4 run and the baselines were measured with outside tools (openssl speed, xxhsum -b, clhash's own benchmark), so this stays at C.

name: Intel(R) Multi-Buffer Crypto for IPsec (intel-ipsec-mb)
baseline: OpenSSL (AES-256-CBC+HMAC-SHA-256 throughput) and FreeBSD OpenCrypto Framework (OCF) default kernel crypto (AES-GCM / ChaCha20-Poly1305 VPN throughput)
workload: Raw AES-256-CBC+HMAC-SHA-256 throughput vs OpenSSL on an AVX2 host, plus end-to-end iperf3 VPN throughput (OpenVPN DCO, IPsec-ESP, WireGuard) in pfSense/FreeBSD with an IIMB-based engine replacing OCF as the in-kernel crypto provider
claimed_speedup: Netgate AsiaBSDCon 2023 paper: on an AVX2 test host, IPsec-MB did 18.1 Gbps AES-256-CBC+HMAC-SHA-256 on 1400-byte blocks vs OpenSSL's maximum of 10.4 Gbps on 16 kB blocks, about 1.7x (derived from page data). In pfSense/FreeBSD VPN tests, the IIMB engine was compared with FreeBSD's default OpenCrypto Framework (OCF) on Ryzen 5 5600 VMs: OpenVPN DCO AES-256-GCM async 10 vs 6.0 Gbps; ChaCha20-Poly1305 async 7.0 vs 4.10 Gbps; IPsec-ESP AES-128-GCM async 7.68 vs 4.46 Gbps. On the Netgate SG-8200 (Atom C3758), OpenVPN AES-256-GCM async was 2.50 vs 1.50 Gbps.
hardware: OpenSSL comparison: unnamed 'test host with AVX2'. VPN tests: AMD Ryzen 5 5600 (KVM/QEMU VMs running FreeBSD-CURRENT) and Netgate SG-8200 (Intel Atom C3758).
stars_or_usage: 339 stars; used as the software crypto backend in DPDK, Intel(R) QAT Engine, and FD.io
tradeoffs: Job-based multi-buffer API is a different programming model than OpenSSL's EVP interface (best throughput requires batching many buffers together); x86-64/AArch64 specific, hand-written per-ISA assembly; targets IPsec/packet-processing workloads rather than general-purpose drop-in crypto.
caveats: The only OpenSSL head-to-head is one sentence in a downstream user's (Netgate) paper. It covers AES-256-CBC+HMAC-SHA-256, not AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, uses mismatched block sizes (1400 B for IPsec-MB vs 16 kB for OpenSSL), and names no CPU model or compiler. The AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 gains are measured against FreeBSD's OCF framework, not OpenSSL, in end-to-end VPN throughput, so part of the gain comes from the new engine's job batching and async handling, not only the library's kernels. The paper's ARM (SG-1100) results use ISA-L AES and OpenSSL ChaCha20-Poly1305, not intel-ipsec-mb. Intel's own white paper (2012) and the DPDK 25.11 Intel crypto performance report give absolute throughput only, with no OpenSSL comparison. The vendored ML-DSA/ML-KEM code is Apache-2.0 (LICENSE.OpenSSL); the rest is BSD-3-Clause, and both are OSI-approved.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos ipp-crypto (led to intel/isa-l_crypto, then to sibling repo intel/intel-ipsec-mb)

name: blake2b_simd / blake2s_simd
baseline: OpenSSL SHA-512 / OpenSSL SHA-1 (also compared to libsodium BLAKE2b)
workload: 1,000,000-byte in-memory inputs hashed by BLAKE3, blake2b_simd/blake2s_simd (single, many::hash, BLAKE2bp/BLAKE2sp), libsodium BLAKE2b and OpenSSL SHA-1/SHA-512. Each algorithm runs in 100 worker processes across all 512 input offsets. Total time is averaged (a mean, not a median) and reported as cycles per byte (benches/bench_multiprocess).
claimed_speedup: blake2b_simd BLAKE2b: 2.81 cpb vs OpenSSL SHA-512: 5.11 cpb (~1.8x); vs OpenSSL SHA-1: 3.51 cpb (~1.25x); vs libsodium BLAKE2b: 3.07 cpb (~1.09x). blake2s_simd many::hash: 1.31 cpb, blake2b_simd many::hash: 1.43 cpb
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.40.0, `cargo run --release` (default release profile with no target-cpu flag; the crate picks SIMD paths by runtime CPU-feature detection). clang 9.0.1 was used only for Samuel Neves' blake2-avx2 C reference, built with `-mavx2` in benches/blake2-avx2-sneves/build.rs. OpenSSL 1.1.1d and libsodium 1.0.18 were linked through the openssl and libsodium-ffi crates, and the build flags of those libraries are not stated.
hardware: Intel Core i5-8250U (Kaby Lake Refresh)
stars_or_usage: 144 stars; crates.io: blake2b_simd ~57.8M downloads, blake2s_simd ~23.0M downloads
tradeoffs: Pure Rust with dynamic AVX2 CPU-feature detection at runtime; SIMD kernel is a Rust port of Samuel Neves' sneves/blake2-avx2 C code. Not C++-native (usable from C++ only via FFI/cbindgen), no_std support optional. Benchmark numbers are from 2019-2020 hardware (i5-8250U, OpenSSL 1.1.1d), so absolute cycles/byte on current CPUs/OpenSSL 3.x will differ, though the relative BLAKE2b-vs-SHA-512 gap is architectural and should persist.

The bench crate has since been updated (edition 2024, blake3 1.8.3), so a rerun today uses different code and toolchains. The main comparison crosses algorithms. BLAKE2b, BLAKE2bp and many::hash are not drop-in replacements for SHA-512/SHA-1, since they produce different digests, and BLAKE2bp is a separate parallel mode. Against the same algorithm (libsodium BLAKE2b, 3.07 cpb), the win is only ~1.09x (derived from page data). The i5-8250U has no SHA-NI, so OpenSSL SHA-1 ran without hardware SHA extensions, and the margin would be smaller on SHA-NI CPUs. The bench code measures nanoseconds, and the README does not say how it converted them to cpb. Only first-party runs on a single machine exist.

name: BLAKE3
baseline: SHA-256 and SHA3-256: the fastest of SUPERCOP's implementations, whose candidates include OpenSSL-backed ones. BLAKE2b is also compared. The project's own chart used OpenSSL 1.1.1d SHA-256/SHA3-256 and BLAKE2b via blake2b_simd.
workload: Single-core, long-message hashing throughput in cycles/byte. eBASH defines this as 1/16384 of the cycle difference between 18208-byte and 1824-byte messages, taking the median of many runs.
claimed_speedup: eBASH long-message medians on 'panther' (Intel Core i7-1165G7, Tiger Lake, SUPERCOP 20260831): BLAKE3 0.51 cycles/byte vs SHA-256 2.21 (~4.3x), SHA3-256 5.50 (~10.8x), BLAKE2b 2.99 (~5.9x). Ratios are derived from page data. Each figure is the fastest SUPERCOP implementation of that primitive, and the candidates include the OpenSSL-backed sha256/sha3256 implementations. At 1536-byte messages BLAKE3 (2.88 c/b) is slower than SHA-256 (2.34 c/b) on this SHA-NI CPU.
compiler_and_flags: SUPERCOP 20260831. The eBASH implementation page lists the best build per implementation: crypto_hash/blake3/avx512 used clang -mcpu=native -O3 -fwrapv -Qunused-arguments -fPIC -fPIE (Debian Clang 14.0.6); the sha256/openssl wrapper used gcc -march=native -mtune=native -O2 -fwrapv -fPIC -fPIE and links the system OpenSSL (version not stated). The long-message table does not say which implementation or compiler produced each best figure.
hardware: eBASH 'panther': Intel Core i7-1165G7 (Tiger Lake, AVX-512 + SHA-NI, 2.8 GHz). Also eBASH 'hertz': AMD Ryzen 7 7700 (Zen 4).
license: CC0-1.0 OR Apache-2.0 OR Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception
tradeoffs: Different digest from SHA-2/SHA-3/BLAKE2 (not a bit-compatible drop-in); Merkle-tree construction parallelizes across threads and SIMD lanes; official optimized implementations in Rust and C; explicitly not recommended for password hashing.

name: sha2-with-c-intrinsic (AWS Crypto Algorithms Group)
baseline: OpenSSL SHA-256/SHA-512 x86-64 perlasm assembly (AVX and AVX2 paths, plus the SHA-NI path for SHA-256 only), copied into the repo from OpenSSL master as of Feb 24 2020 (README link text says 13c5d744, but the URL points to commit e32c608e)
workload: Full SHA-256/SHA-512 hashing through the same sha256()/sha512() wrapper, switching only the compression backend (C intrinsics vs OpenSSL asm), on message sizes from 1 to 65536 bytes. Each function gets 25 warm-up runs, then 100 timed iterations averaged, and each experiment is repeated 10 times with the minimum reported, in CPU cycles (tests/main_speed.c).
claimed_speedup: SHA-256 w/ Intel SHA Extensions, 65536-byte input: 183,685 cycles (their C intrinsics) vs 198,528 cycles (OpenSSL SHA-NI asm) = ~1.08x faster (derived from page data). Their generic/AVX/AVX2/AVX-512 C paths are NOT faster than OpenSSL's corresponding avx/avx2 asm paths on the same table (e.g. avx2 (C) 709,146 cycles vs avx2 (ossl) 620,729 cycles at 65536 bytes -- OpenSSL wins there).
compiler_and_flags: clang-9, CMake Release build with TEST_SPEED. cmake/compilation-flags.cmake sets -O3 -march=native -mno-red-zone -fPIC -std=c99 -ggdb, not -O2. The OpenSSL .s files are assembled into the same binary. The repo was also built and tested with gcc-9.
hardware: Dell XPS 13 7390 2-in-1, Intel Core i7-1065G7 (Ice Lake), Turbo Boost off, Ubuntu 18.04.2 LTS
tradeoffs: Provides only raw compression functions (no padding/state management, no shared/static lib); explicitly a benchmarking/compiler-research sample, not intended for production use. Requires SHA_NI/AVX/AVX2/AVX512 capable CPU and matching compiler intrinsics support.
caveats: This is a mixed result. Only the SHA-256 SHA-NI C path beats OpenSSL: ~1.05-1.08x at 64 bytes and up (424 vs 446 cycles at 64 B, 183,685 vs 198,528 at 65536 B), and it ties at 32 bytes or less (281 vs 280 at 32 B, derived from page data). Every AVX/AVX2 C path, and all of SHA-512 (which has no SHA-NI path), loses to OpenSSL's asm, e.g. SHA-512 avx2 456,221 vs 402,204 cycles at 65536 B. The authors frame the repo as compiler feedback: they say C built with gcc-9/clang-9 'is often slower than the performance of hand written assembly code'. It ships only test binaries, with no shared or static library, and is 'designed to be used for benchmarking purposes only and not in final products'. The numbers are from 2020, against an unreleased OpenSSL master snapshot, on one Ice Lake laptop built with -march=native. The repo has had a single commit (2020-05-31) and is abandoned. The authors are Drucker & Gueron (AWS Crypto Algorithms Group).

The stdlib baseline itself already uses the ARMv8 SHA-2 instructions on Apple Silicon, so the gain comes from 4-way multi-buffer interleaving, not from hardware SHA versus software SHA.

name: hashtree
workload: Batched SHA-256 compression of many 64-byte blocks per call (1/4/8/16 blocks at once) for Merkle-tree / beacon-chain hashing, built with HAVE_OPENSSL=1 to benchmark directly against OpenSSL's native SHA-256
claimed_speedup: Unnamed x86-64 CPU without SHA extensions: OpenSSL SHA256() called one message at a time takes 30.519 ms, vs 6.519 ms for avx_x8 (AVX2, 8 blocks per call). That is about 4.7x (derived from page data); the README says '5 times faster'. Banana Pi BPI-R3, which the README describes as RISC-V: OpenSSL takes 465.372 ms vs 109.428 ms for riscv_zbb_x1, about 4.25x (derived from page data); the README says '450% improvement'. The Cascade Lake avx_x16 figure of 2.413 ms vs about 28.8 ms for a single block is about 12x, but against the library's own x1 kernel, not OpenSSL. The Go-binding benchmarks are about 6-11x faster than Prysm's earlier Go implementation (derived from page data), also not OpenSSL.
compiler_and_flags: gcc/gas (Apple clang on Apple Silicon) via src/Makefile with CFLAGS -g -Wall -Werror -O3; RISC-V builds add -march=rv64gc_zbb_zk. HAVE_OPENSSL=1 links the system OpenSSL. The compiler and OpenSSL versions are not stated.
hardware: Direct OpenSSL comparisons: an unnamed x86-64 CPU without SHA extensions (AVX2-capable), and a Banana Pi BPI-R3 that the README describes as having a RISC-V processor. Rows without OpenSSL: an unnamed Cascade Lake AVX-512 host and a Raspberry Pi 4 Model B. Go comparisons against Prysm: AMD Ryzen 5 3600, Intel Core i5-3570 and i5-7200U.
stars_or_usage: 42 stars. The status-im/nimbus-eth2 source references hashtree through its Nim bindings. Prysm's go.mod depends on the separate Go-assembly port prysmaticlabs/gohashtree (25 stars), not on C bindings of this repo.
tradeoffs: Only wins when many independent 64-byte blocks (Merkle-tree leaves) can be hashed together; a single hash call is no faster than OpenSSL. Requires SIMD (AVX2/AVX-512/SHA-NI/NEON). Low-level C API (raw pointers, fixed sizes, no bounds checking); caller owns all buffers.
caveats: Both direct OpenSSL comparisons come from underspecified hardware: an x86 CPU identified only as lacking SHA extensions, and a board the README calls a 'Banana Pi BPI-R3 with a RISC-V processor'. The OpenSSL case calls the one-shot SHA256() once per 64-byte message, single-buffer, while hashtree takes many blocks per call. The gap is therefore mainly multi-buffer vs single-buffer, and on SHA-NI CPUs, where OpenSSL uses SHA-NI, no same-run OpenSSL number is given. The Cascade Lake and Raspberry Pi rows have no OpenSSL column. No compiler or OpenSSL versions are given.

name: j-lanes tree hashing mode and j-lanes SHA-256 (Gueron)
workload: SHA-256 hashing of single messages ranging 2KB-132KB, using a 4-lanes SIMD tree-hashing mode (j=4) on AVX, versus standard serial SHA-256
claimed_speedup: 4-lanes SHA-256 is 1.97-2.53x faster than OpenSSL 1.0.1c for 2KB-128KB messages (Fig. 3: 13.27 vs 6.75 c/B at 2KB; 12.78 vs 5.05 c/B at 128KB). The abstract gives ~2 to ~2.5x. Against the fastest serial implementation (the authors' own n-SMS) it is 1.5-1.97x per the abstract and 1.55-2x per Sec. 3. At 8KB it is also faster than tree-mode BLAKE and Keccak (Fig. 4).
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 (3rd Gen Core, Ivy Bridge, AVX), with Hyper-Threading, Turbo Boost and Enhanced SpeedStep disabled
tradeoffs: Requires restructuring hashing into a tree mode (message split into j independent SIMD lanes, then combined), which changes the digest unless both hasher and verifier use the same mode; needs AVX; author was an Intel researcher and later pushed related multi-buffer techniques toward OpenSSL/ISA-L.
caveats: j-lanes SHA-256 is a different hash construction: a tree mode whose digest differs from standard SHA-256, and the paper itself says it would need distinct IVs if standardized. It is not a drop-in replacement for OpenSSL SHA-256. The 'fastest publicly available' comparator is the author's own n-SMS code. No compiler or flags are stated and no code is released. The results are from 2012 hardware against OpenSSL 1.0.1c, which predates OpenSSL's AVX2 and SHA-NI SHA-256 paths. The peer-reviewed venue is a SCIRP journal, a publisher whose review standards are widely questioned.
found_via: IACR ePrint site search "SHA-256 SIMD faster" -> https://eprint.iacr.org/2012/476, opened and read PDF via curl+pdftotext

verification.tier_reason: The paper measures 4-lanes SHA-256 against OpenSSL 1.0.1c on an i7-3770 (Figs. 1-3: 12.78-13.27 vs 5.05-6.75 cycles/byte, 1.97-2.53x). It was peer-review published as Journal of Information Security 4(1):7-11, 2013 (DOI 10.4236/jis.2013.41002), with the same abstract numbers. There is no public code and no compiler or flags, so it is not A.
verification.notes: The claimed numbers check out against both the ePrint PDF and the JIS 2013 abstract. The main issue for enrichment is that j-lanes changes the digest, so this is a new hash mode, not a faster SHA-256. B rests on the JIS (SCIRP) publication; if the orchestrator does not count SCIRP as peer review, it drops to C.

name: libsodium (BLAKE2b)
workload: BLAKE2b one-shot hashing of 64/256/1024/4096/16384-byte buffers using Google Benchmark, with Crypto++ 8.9.0, OpenSSL 3.6.0, Botan 3.9.0, libsodium 1.0.20 and mbedTLS 4.0.0 all statically linked and built with identical compiler flags
claimed_speedup: libsodium's BLAKE2b beats OpenSSL's BLAKE2b at small-to-medium sizes (means of 5 repetitions): ~2.70x at 64B (577.8 vs 213.7 MB/s), ~1.91x at 256B (1243.6 vs 650.3 MB/s), ~1.18x at 1024B (1307.0 vs 1107.2 MB/s), about tied at 4096B (1338.4 vs 1333.9 MB/s); OpenSSL retakes the lead by ~4% at 16384B (1402.7 vs 1349.3 MB/s) (all derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: The README says -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -flto -funroll-loops -fomit-frame-pointer (PGO optional) is applied to all libraries. However, cmake/FetchLibsodium.cmake configures libsodium with CFLAGS=${CMAKE_C_FLAGS_RELEASE}, not the shared CRYPTO_BENCH_C_FLAGS that OpenSSL gets, so libsodium's flags probably differ. result.json does not record the compiler, its version, or whether PGO was used.
hardware: Host 'sccdeMacBook-Air.local' (Apple Silicon MacBook Air; the chip model is not named), 8 logical CPUs. The result.json context block reports 64KB L1D / 128KB L1I / 4MB L2, a release build, and a run dated 2025-11-05.
tradeoffs: libsodium's crypto_generichash BLAKE2b API differs from OpenSSL's EVP interface; the advantage shrinks and reverses as the buffer grows past ~8KB, so it is a small-message win rather than an across-the-board one.
caveats: This is a harvested shootout result, not a claim libsodium makes about itself. It is a single local run (2025-11-05) on a MacBook Air by the author of an obscure 0-star benchmark repo; the CPU model and compiler are not recorded. The small-size gap is inflated by the harness: the OpenSSL adapter calls EVP_MD_CTX_new, EVP_DigestInit_ex(EVP_blake2b512()) and EVP_MD_CTX_free on every hash, while libsodium makes one crypto_generichash_blake2b call. The 64-256B gains therefore mostly measure OpenSSL EVP per-call overhead rather than the BLAKE2b compression function, and at 16KB OpenSSL is ~4% faster. The README says flags are identical, but the build scripts pass libsodium CMAKE_C_FLAGS_RELEASE rather than the shared -march=native/-flto flags.

name: LSH-256 / LSH-512 (Korean hash standard, TTAK.KO-12.0276)
baseline: BLAKE2 (BLAKE2b vs LSH-512, BLAKE2s vs LSH-256) and SHA-3 (SHA3-512 / SHA3-256). Each eBASH row is the fastest SUPERCOP implementation of that function. For SHA-3 the winner is 'oncore64bits'; OpenSSL's SHA-3 is also measured and is 1.27-1.28x slower.
workload: eBASH/SUPERCOP crypto_hash timings on amd64-alder. Long-message cycles/byte is 1/16384 of the cycle-count difference between hashing 18208-byte and 1824-byte messages (per the page). Rows are medians (StQ2) of many measurements. The page also lists 8/64/576/1536/4096-byte figures.
claimed_speedup: eBASH amd64-alder (Core i3-12100), long-message medians: LSH-512 2.14 cycles/byte vs BLAKE2b 3.36 (~1.57x) and SHA3-512 11.25 (~5.26x); LSH-256 3.13 vs BLAKE2s 5.24 (~1.67x) and SHA3-256 5.96 (~1.90x) (ratios derived from page data). Both variants also win at 576-4096 bytes but lose at 64 bytes (LSH-512 9.52, LSH-256 7.27 vs BLAKE2b 7.04, BLAKE2s 4.84 cycles/byte). BLAKE3 (1.73) and SHA-256 (2.05) are faster than both LSH variants on long messages. SUPERCOP's Crypto++-derived 'cryptopp' implementation is 2.92x slower than the best LSH-512 (11240 vs 3854 in the test-results Time column), which is ~2.2x slower than BLAKE2b's best (5142) but still ~1.56x faster than SHA3-512 (17498). For LSH-256 it is only 1.05x slower than the best (5503), still ~1.46x faster than BLAKE2s (8016) and ~1.74x faster than SHA3-256 (9597) (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Per implementation on alder (SUPERCOP keeps the fastest compiler/flag combination; all use -fwrapv -fPIC -fPIE). LSH-512 avx2: Debian Clang 19.1.7 -march=native -O2. LSH-256 ssse3: Clang 19.1.7 -march=native -Os. BLAKE2b regs: gcc 14.2.0 -march=native -mtune=native -O. BLAKE2s avxicc: Clang 19.1.7 -march=native -O. SHA3-512 oncore64bits: gcc 14.2.0 -march=native -mtune=native -O2. SHA3-256 oncore64bits: gcc 14.2.0 -O3. Crypto++-derived LSH-512: g++ -march=native -mtune=native -O. Crypto++-derived LSH-256: clang++ -march=native -O3.
hardware: amd64-alder eBACS test machine: 2022 Intel Core i3-12100 (Golden Cove, model 90675-00), 4x3300MHz, supercop-20260831
license: BSL-1.0 (the Crypto++ compilation is under the Boost Software License 1.0; individual files, including lsh256*/lsh512*.cpp, are placed in the public domain)
tradeoffs: LSH uses a wider 128-byte block and a generalized-Feistel structure unrelated to Merkle-Damgard SHA-2 or sponge-based SHA-3/BLAKE2; far fewer independent implementations, audits, and years of cryptanalysis than SHA-2/SHA-3/BLAKE2. Only actively-maintained C/C++ library implementation found is Crypto++ (SSE2/AVX2 code, header cites Korea Internet & Security Agency spec).
caveats: The eBASH headline numbers come from SUPERCOP's own avx2 (LSH-512) and ssse3 (LSH-256) implementations, not from Crypto++. SUPERCOP also benchmarks a 'cryptopp' LSH implementation: on alder it is 2.92x slower than the best for LSH-512, which puts it behind BLAKE2b, and 1.05x slower for LSH-256. It is not known whether that build uses Crypto++'s lsh512_avx.cpp path. Crypto++'s LSH code (lsh256/lsh512 .cpp plus _sse/_avx) was written by Jeffrey Walton from KISA's specification and reference code. LSH loses to BLAKE2 on short (64-byte and 8-byte) messages, and BLAKE3 and SHA-NI SHA-256 beat it on long messages on this CPU. IACR eprint 2015/494 (withdrawn) described free-start collision and pseudo-preimage attacks on full-round LSH, possible because LSH has no feed-forward, plus 14-round boomerang attacks; none is a practical collision on the standard hash. The ISO/IEC 10118-3 inclusion claim was not verified. The Crypto++ compilation is BSL-1.0 and the individual files are public domain.

corrected_fields.caveats: The eBACS/SUPERCOP cycles-per-byte numbers are from SUPERCOP's own bundled LSH implementation (submitted by/derived from the KISA designers), not confirmed to be byte-identical to Crypto++'s AVX2 code, though Crypto++ is cited here as the actively-maintained, permissively-licensed C++ implementation of the same standardized algorithm (LSH-512, Korean standard KS X 3262, also ISO/IEC 10118-3:2018). name: Simultaneous hashing of multiple messages / S-HASH (Gueron & Krasnov)
workload: 4-buffer parallel (multi-buffer) SHA-256 hashing of multiple independent messages, measured from CPU cache/memory and from disk
claimed_speedup: From L1/L2/LLC/memory (4KB messages): 5.18-5.21 c/B vs OpenSSL 1.0.1 at 17.72-17.80 c/B, 3.42x, and 2.25x vs the authors' own n-SMS serial code. From disk at the native 3.3GHz: 2.26x (UNIFORM directory, 8.65 vs 19.55 c/B) and 1.73x (DIVERSE directory). The abstract's '~6.73 c/B, almost 3x' figure is with the CPU down-clocked to 1.6GHz (UNIFORM: 6.73 vs 19.26 c/B, 2.86x).
hardware: Intel Core i5-2500 (Sandy Bridge, 3.3GHz; some disk runs down-clocked to 2.6/1.7/1.6GHz), Turbo Boost, Hyper-Threading and SpeedStep disabled, 8GB DDR3-1600, RAID0 of two Intel SSD 320, Fedora 16
tradeoffs: Only pays off when multiple independent messages/buffers can be hashed concurrently (e.g. boot-time integrity checks, multi-stream server workloads); unlike j-lanes (2012/476), gives no benefit for a single serial message.
caveats: Applies only when many independent messages are available: each message still gets a standard SHA-256 digest, but a single message is not sped up (see j-lanes for that). OpenSSL RT ticket 2784 is the authors' n-SMS patch (the faster serial comparator), not S-HASH itself. No S-HASH code is released and no compiler or flags are stated. The disk results are bound by the SSDs, and the ~3x disk figure needs a down-clocked CPU. OpenSSL later shipped its own multi-buffer SHA-256 (crypto/sha/asm/sha256-mb-x86_64.pl, Polyakov, (c) 2013, used for multi-block AES-CBC-HMAC), so the incumbent absorbed the technique for that use. The results are from 2012 hardware against OpenSSL 1.0.1. The peer-reviewed venue is a SCIRP journal.
found_via: IACR ePrint site search "SHA-256 SIMD faster" -> https://eprint.iacr.org/2012/371, opened and read PDF via curl+pdftotext

verification.tier_reason: The paper benchmarks 4-buffer S-HASH SHA-256 against serial OpenSSL 1.0.1 on a Core i5-2500 (Fig. 2: 17.72-17.80 vs 5.18-5.21 c/B, i.e. 3.42x; Figs. 3-4 for disk). It was peer-review published as Journal of Information Security 3(4):319-325, 2012 (DOI 10.4236/jis.2012.34039). There is no code and no compiler or flags, so it is not A.
verification.notes: The record's '~3x from disk at 6.73 c/B' omitted that this is at a 1.6GHz down-clock; at native frequency it is 2.26x. I rewrote the claim with the full numbers, and the tier stands. The RT 2784 caveat was misattributed and is fixed. B rests on the JIS (SCIRP) publication, and without it this would be C.

name: blake2b-simd (Minio)
baseline: The package's own pure-Go BLAKE2b fallback (compress_generic.go, derived from dchest/blake2b), labelled 'go.txt' in the benchcmp output. Also compared against Go stdlib crypto/md5, crypto/sha1, crypto/sha256 and crypto/sha512.
workload: Size benchmarks hash 64B-128KB buffers on one core on amd64 (AVX2/AVX/SSE assembly vs the pure-Go path). The stdlib comparison benchmark hashes 1 MiB messages, written in 1 KiB chunks.
claimed_speedup: AVX2 is 3.94x faster than the pure-Go path at 128K (233.37 -> 918.93 MB/s); the README calls this 'roughly 4X ... approaching 1GB/sec on a single core'. AVX is 3.28x and SSE 2.85x at 128K, on a MacBook Pro i7. In the comparison benchmark, BLAKE2b-simd runs at 850.64 MB/s vs stdlib SHA-256 at 189.58 MB/s (~4.5x, derived from page data), SHA-512 at 306.33 MB/s and MD5 at 607.48 MB/s.
stars_or_usage: 255 stars; used internally by Minio for bitrot detection in its erasure-coded object storage
tradeoffs: Requires AVX2/AVX/SSE (auto-selects, falls back to generic); Go-assembly implementation increases maintenance burden; BLAKE2b is a different digest/algorithm than SHA-2, not a drop-in replacement where SHA-2 compliance (e.g. FIPS) is required.
caveats: Benchmarks compare only against the package's own pure-Go fallback and Go's stdlib hashes, not against OpenSSL or libb2 BLAKE2b. The stdlib SHA-256 baseline is from the 2016-era Go, before SHA-NI support, so its ratio is inflated compared with modern hardware or toolchains. The repo is archived by GitHub and the last commit on master is 2016-07-23 (pushed_at 2017-11-27). The Go compiler version is not stated for the benchmarks (CI tested Go 1.5/1.6). name: Intel ISA-L Crypto (multi-buffer SHA)
baseline: The best-known single-buffer SHA-256 of 2012. The whitepaper cites Intel's own 'Fast SHA-256 Implementations on Intel Architecture Processors' (Guilford, Yap, Gopal, May 2012; ref [4]). OpenSSL is not named.
workload: Multi-Hash SHA-256 (SHA256x4) of a single 1 MB buffer on one core with Hyper-Threading and Turbo Boost off. SHA256x4 is a tree-mode extension that interleaves one buffer across 4 SIMD lanes and then hashes the lane digests, so its output is not a standard SHA-256 digest. Timing is rdtsc cycles/byte, using the trimmed mean of many runs.
claimed_speedup: ~5 cycles/byte for Multi-Hash SHA-256 on a 1 MB buffer, 'over 2X faster than the best known SHA-256 single buffer implementations' (Executive Summary). The Results section says SHA256x4 Multi-Hash gives a '~2.6X performance gain over the best SHA256 algorithm computation' at 1 MB, and MD5 Multi-Hash (x8) gives '~4.4X'.
hardware: Intel Core i7-2600 (Sandy Bridge), single core with Intel HT Technology, Turbo Boost off
tradeoffs: Only accelerates throughput when multiple independent buffers can be scheduled concurrently; needs application-level batching (not a transparent single-call speedup); requires NASM/gas for the hand-written SIMD kernels.
caveats: The only published performance source is Intel's own July 2012 Multi-Hash whitepaper, run on a Core i7-2600 that predates SHA-NI. Its baseline is Intel's best-known single-buffer SHA-256 code (ref [4]), not OpenSSL, and it states no compiler or flags. It measures Multi-Hash, a tree-mode SHA-256 variant whose digest is not interoperable with standard SHA-256, in a 4-lane (SHA256x4) layout. The shipped mh_sha256 uses 16 segments (ISAL_HASH_SEGS 16), so the paper's figures do not describe the current code. The library's standard-digest multi-buffer SHA-256 (sha256_mb) has no published numbers. The repo does ship OpenSSL head-to-head perf harnesses (sha256_mb/sha256_mb_vs_ossl_perf.c, sha1_mb/sha1_mb_vs_ossl_perf.c) but commits no results. No modern comparison against OpenSSL with SHA extensions was found.
found_via: Followed from the j-lanes/S-HASH multi-buffer literature (2012/476, 2012/371) to intel/isa-l_crypto, which implements the same multi-buffer technique; read README and linked wiki white paper via curl+pdftotext
GitHub: gh api repos/intel/isa-l_crypto (query 'sha256 multi-buffer intel'), then linked wiki whitepaper PDF (multi-hash-paper.pdf) via curl+pdftotext

GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION, but the root LICENSE file is BSD-3-Clause (it carries an SPDX line). The usage claims in stars_or_usage were not checked.

name: KangarooTwelve (XKCP)
baseline: SHAKE128 (FIPS 202), SHA-256 and SHA-512, using the fastest implementations available to the authors, cross-checked with eBASH; 'often' OpenSSL for the traditional hashes
workload: Single-core hashing of long messages (much larger than 8 KiB) in cycles/byte. K12 uses its 8 KiB-leaf tree mode with 4-way AVX2 or 8-way AVX-512 Keccak-p[1600,12]. The <=8 KiB row is serial.
claimed_speedup: Paper Table 2 (single core, long messages, cycles/byte): KangarooTwelve runs at 0.55 on a Core i7-7800X (SkylakeX), 1.22 on a Core i5-6500 (Skylake) and 1.44 on a Core i5-4570 (Haswell). SHAKE128 runs at 4.28/5.56/7.09 (K12 ~7.8x/~4.6x/~4.9x faster) and SHA-256 at 6.65/6.91/9.27 (~12x/~5.7x/~6.4x). Serial K12 (<=8 KiB) runs at 2.35/2.89/3.68, still ~1.8-1.9x faster than SHAKE128. Ratios are derived from page data.
hardware: Intel Core i7-7800X (SkylakeX, AVX-512), Core i5-6500 (Skylake), Core i5-4570 (Haswell)
license: CC0-1.0 for most files, with per-file exceptions: CRYPTOGAMS BSD-style/GPL (AVX2 and AVX-512 KeccakP-1600 asm), Apache-2.0 OR ISC OR MIT (ARMv8-A cores), and Brian Gladman's permissive license (brg_endian.h)
stars_or_usage: 664 stars; official Keccak-team code, basis for the SHA-3/Keccak reference and optimized implementations used across the ecosystem
tradeoffs: KangarooTwelve (12-round Keccak-p variant) is an XOF, not a drop-in SHA-3/SHAKE replacement -- smaller security margin (12 vs 24 rounds) in exchange for speed; needs the XKCP AVX2/AVX-512 target build to hit the stated numbers.
caveats: The paper's authors are K12's designers, and its 2016-2018 hardware predates SHA-NI. The keccak.team page gives KT128 at 1.4 c/b with AVX2 and 0.51 c/b with AVX-512, and 0.75 c/b on Apple A14/M1 with ARMv8-A SHA-3 instructions (1.7x hardware SHA-256, 3x hardware SHA-512). That page's 'roughly twice faster than SHAKE128' applies to low-end platforms and short messages, not to the AVX2/AVX-512 figures. Independent eBASH 2026 data at ~16 KiB (too short for K12's 8 KiB-leaf parallelism to be fully used) tells a different story. On a Core i7-1165G7, K12 runs at 2.47 c/b vs SHA-256 at 2.21, so K12 is slower than SHA-NI SHA-256, though ~1.8x faster than SHAKE128 (4.49) and ~2.2x faster than SHA3-256 (5.50). On a Ryzen 7 7700 it runs at 2.93 vs SHA-256 at 2.02. No compiler or flags are stated in the paper or on the page. The fast x86 AVX2/AVX-512 cores are CRYPTOGAMS-licensed rather than CC0, and the CC0 parts carry no patent grant.

name: sha256-simd (minio)
workload: Single-core SHA256 hashing of 8B-10MB buffers (the Performance table uses >1MB blocks): the package's ARM64 path against Go crypto/sha256 on a Cortex-A53, and its AVX512 and SHA-Ext paths against its own AVX2 path on x86.
claimed_speedup: Against Go crypto/sha256 (the README's 'golang' column), the ARM64 path on a 1.2GHz Cortex-A53 (Pine64) is 8.38x at 8B, 57.75x at 1KB, 95.11x at 8KB and 105.49x at 1MB (638.23 vs 6.05 MB/s). That Go version predates stdlib ARM64 SHA2 support. The x86 figures are package-internal: AVX512 3498.20 vs its own AVX2 path 448.62 MB/s (7.80x, BenchmarkHash5M, 3.0GHz Xeon Platinum 8124M), and SHA Extensions 1975.17 vs its own AVX2 path 514.40 MB/s (3.84x, BenchmarkHash5M, 3.7GHz Ryzen 7 2700X per the README Performance table).
hardware: 3.0 GHz Intel Xeon Platinum 8124M (AVX512); 3.7 GHz AMD Ryzen 7 2700X (SHA Extensions); 1.2 GHz ARM Cortex-A53 (Pine64). The Celeron J3455 is only named as a SHA-Ext-capable CPU, not as a benchmark host.
stars_or_usage: 1.0k stars; used in the MinIO object storage server for multipart-upload integrity checks
tradeoffs: AVX512 mode requires explicit multi-buffer scheduling (Avx512Server/channels) and only pays off with many concurrent ~5MB-sized SHA256 calls; no benefit for small or single messages; Go-only, not callable from C++.
caveats: The Go stdlib has since caught up. crypto/sha256 gained an optimized arm64 (SHA2-instruction) implementation in a 2017-11-14 commit and a SHA-NI amd64 implementation in a 2023-03-31 commit. Issue #76 (Dec 2025) shows Go 1.25.5 stdlib matching or slightly beating the package's ARM path on an Apple M1 Max. The remaining edge is the AVX512 16-lane multi-buffer path, which is ported from Intel intel-ipsec-mb, needs an explicit Avx512Server and many concurrent goroutines, and is slower for messages under 1MB. It was never benchmarked against modern stdlib SHA-NI. The x86 README numbers are against the package's own AVX2 path, not the stdlib. No commits since 2023-02-22 (about 3.6 years), so it is flagged abandoned.

name: aklomp/base64 (SIMD Base64 C99 library)
workload: Single-threaded base64 decode of real files (images, text, 1.4-330 KB) with error checking, from the Muła & Lemire paper; plus encode/decode of a 1 MB buffer from the Turbo-Base64 README shootout
claimed_speedup: Muła & Lemire (ACM TWEB 2018) Table VI, decode on real files: AVX2 (Klomp) 0.43 cycles/byte vs Google Chrome base64 1.8 and Linux kernel base64 20 on lena.jpg (~4.2x vs Chrome, ~46x vs Linux, derived from page data). Also Turbo-Base64 README (1 MB buffer, i7-9700K, gcc 11.2): b64avx2 26,153 MB/s encode / 22,515 MB/s decode vs Google Chrome base64 2,541/4,289 MB/s (~10x encode, ~5x decode, derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.3 -O3 -march=native (Muła & Lemire paper, lemire/fastbase64 Makefile adds -mavx2). The Turbo-Base64 table states only gcc 11.2, with no flags given for the competitor builds
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 (Skylake) @ 3.4 GHz, Turbo Boost disabled (paper); Intel i7-9700K @ 3.6 GHz (Turbo-Base64 table)
tradeoffs: C99 API; OpenMP option for extra parallel speedup; no NEON tuning as aggressive as competitors
caveats: The paper benchmarks a 2017 copy of aklomp's AVX2 decoder vendored into lemire/fastbase64 ('based on Alfred Klomp's code with minor modifications'), decode only. The paper's own AVX2 codec is about 2x faster than Klomp's. The Turbo-Base64 numbers come from a competitor's 2022.02 run against aklomp v2022.02, and its comparison harness is not public. The latest commit (2026-07) only touches CI; the last code change was 2025-05.
