name: base64-turbo (hacer-bark)
baseline: base64 (RFC 4648) codecs: Turbo-Base64 (C, the prior fastest known codec) and the Rust default `base64` crate 0.23 (its SIMD path on by default), plus base64-simd and base64-ng, all in the same harness
workload: criterion.rs benchmark (benches/encoding_bench.rs), base64 encode/decode across input sizes 32B-10MB, pinned to one core
claimed_speedup: At 64 KiB (encode/decode, GiB/s): base64-turbo 81.6/106.5 vs Turbo-Base64 80.7/107.8 on AWS c8a.large (AMD EPYC 9R45), and 25.7/36.9 vs 18.2/38.5 on c7i.large (Xeon Platinum 8488C). Against the default `base64` crate it is 81.6/106.5 vs 13.5/27.9 (c8a) and 25.7/36.9 vs 8.9/13.7 (c7i), which is about 6.0x/3.8x and 2.9x/2.7x (derived from page data). The c8a sweep peaks at 123.0 GiB/s encode and 118.1 GiB/s decode at 4 KiB. At that size the raw output has Turbo-Base64 decode at 119.7, so decode is still marginally behind (raw file).
compiler_and_flags: rustc version not stated (MSRV 1.93; the reproduction steps install the current rustup stable). `cargo bench` uses the default bench profile (opt-level 3, no custom RUSTFLAGS or target-cpu; kernels are picked at runtime). Criterion runs with a 5 s warm-up. The README says 15 s of measurement, but encoding_bench.rs actually uses 8/10/12 s depending on the size tier. Turbo-Base64 is compiled through the cc crate in benches/tb64-sys/build.rs with -O3 -DNDEBUG -fstrict-aliasing (-falign-loops on gcc) and upstream's per-file -march flags (ssse3, corei7-avx, haswell, skylake-avx512 -mavx512vbmi). The C compiler and its version are not stated.
hardware: AWS c8a.large (AMD EPYC 9R45, Zen5) and c7i.large (Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C, Sapphire Rapids), pinned to one core
tradeoffs: Pure Rust; SIMD kernels use `unsafe` verified with Kani/MIRI/MSan/fuzzing, scalar fallback is `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`; no published C API/bindings, so a C++ caller would need to write its own FFI shim; custom (non-RFC4648) alphabets lose AVX2/NEON acceleration
caveats: 0BSD carries no explicit patent grant. Results against Turbo-Base64 are mixed. At 64 KiB base64-turbo wins encode but is slightly slower on decode on both machines. Turbo-Base64 also wins 32 B encode, and on c8a it pulls ahead once the data no longer fits in cache (README: about 28% faster encode and 22% faster decode at 10 MB). The clear win is over the Rust default `base64` crate. The author wrote the C-side timing harness and calls those margins 'directional'. Neither the rustc nor the C compiler version is stated. The 100+ GiB/s peaks need AVX-512 VBMI and hold only at 4 KiB. The project is very new with little visibility (2 stars, repo created 2026-01-20), and no one has reproduced the results independently.

name: Fast CRC32 (Sarwate / Slicing-by-8 / Slicing-by-16)
baseline: Classic byte-wise Sarwate table-lookup CRC32 (the author's own crc32_1byte reimplementation). The page says zlib and PHP use this algorithm, but zlib's crc32() itself is not benchmarked.
workload: CRC32 checksum of a 1 GiB in-memory buffer, single-threaded, x86-64 desktop
claimed_speedup: Core i7 860, CRC32 of 1 GByte, figures given as GCC 4.7 / Visual C++ 2010: Slicing-by-8 1800 / 1400 MByte/s; Slicing-by-16 3000 / 2000 MByte/s; Slicing-by-16 4x unrolled with prefetch 3200 / 2000 MByte/s; Slicing-by-4 1050 / 840 MByte/s. The standard Sarwate byte-table implementation runs at 375 MByte/s, so Slicing-by-8 and Slicing-by-16 are about 3.7-8.5x faster than it, and Slicing-by-4 about 2.2-2.8x (derived from page data). The original bitwise version runs at 35 MByte/s.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.7 and Visual C++ 2010. For VC++ the page only says 'full optimization is enabled', and it mentions that GCC -O2 and up unrolls the loop. Exact flags for the published table are not stated. The repo Makefile, added in 2016 after the measurements, uses -O3 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -s.
hardware: Intel Core i7 860 (2.8 GHz, Turbo Boost 3.2 GHz)
tradeoffs: Slicing-by-N trades table memory (up to 16KB) for speed; purely software/table-based, no PCLMULQDQ/SSE4.2 hardware CRC path, so slower than hardware-accelerated CRC32C libraries; single-header C++ library, usable from C via a thin wrapper
caveats: The baseline is a textbook Sarwate byte-table loop, not real zlib. zlib's crc32() has processed four bytes at a time since 1.2.0 in 2003 (the BYFOUR code from Rodney Brown, similar to slicing-by-4, which this page measures at 840-1050 MByte/s). Since 1.2.12 in 2022 zlib uses braided CRC, which its ChangeLog says is 1.5-3x faster again. The speedup over an actual zlib build is therefore much smaller than 3.7-8.5x, and it was never measured. Hardware and compilers are from 2011-2015 (Core i7 860, GCC 4.7, VC++ 2010). There is no PCLMUL/SIMD path, so modern implementations such as zlib-ng and Chromium's zlib are faster. There have been no commits since 2021-09-29.

It is not A for two reasons: the flags used for the 2011-2015 table are never stated (the repo Makefile with -O3 was only added in 2016), and the baseline that was measured is the author's own Sarwate byte-table reimplementation, not zlib's crc32().
verification.notes: Numbers on the page match the record, except that the record's lower ratio bound (~4.3x) is wrong: 1400/375 is about 3.7x, and the record left out the VC++ Slicing-by-16 figure of 2000 MByte/s. The main correction is the baseline: the page equates Sarwate with zlib, but zlib's crc32() has not been byte-wise Sarwate since 2003.

name: fastbase64 (lemire)
baseline: base64 (glibc/Linux base64 utility and Google Chrome's base64 implementation)
workload: Single-threaded base64 decoding of real base64 payloads: the lena, peppers and mandril JPEGs, a Moby Dick quote, and Google and Bing inline images. Secondary: 1 MB encode/decode in the Turbo-Base64 README table.
claimed_speedup: Paper (i7-6700, GCC 5.3 -O3 -march=native): for large random inputs the AVX2 codec uses about 0.25 cycles per input byte, against Chrome's codec at about 2.7 (encode) and 1.8 (decode). The paper calls this 'eleven times faster at encoding and over seven times faster at decoding'. In Table VI, decoding real files takes 0.21-0.27 cycles/byte against Chrome's 1.8-2.1 (lena: 0.21 vs 1.8). In an independent table in the Turbo-Base64 README (i7-9700K, gcc 11.2, 1 MB), fb64avx2 runs at 23,686/21,231 MB/s encode/decode against Google Chrome base64 at 2,541/4,289 MB/s (about 9.3x encode and 4.9x decode, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GNU GCC 5.3, -O3 -march=native (paper; the repo Makefile also sets -O3 -march=native -mavx2). Turbo-Base64 table: gcc 11.2, no flags stated.
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 (Skylake) @ 3.4 GHz, Turbo Boost disabled, 32 GB DDR4-2133 (paper); Intel i7-9700K @ 3.6 GHz (Turbo-Base64 table)
tradeoffs: No declared license (NOASSERTION) — can be studied/reimplemented but not copied; project archived, no further maintenance

The AVX2 codec needs AVX2 hardware and falls back to scalar code for short inputs (under about 100 bytes it gains nothing). Turbo-Base64's source comments call fastbase64 'unsafe, can reads/writes beyound i/o buffers'; that is a competitor's claim and is unverified.

name: crc32c (htot)
baseline: CRC32 (CRC-32C/Castagnoli; SlicingBy8 software baseline is representative of the algorithm used by most CRC32 library implementations)
workload: crc32cbench (crc32c/crc32cbench.cc) on a 4096-byte aligned buffer, as charted; the program also sweeps 16 B to 8 KiB. It compares Sarwate, SlicingBy4, SlicingBy8, Hardware32, Hardware64 (SSE4.2 crc32), Adler (Mark Adler's 3-way crc32), IntelC (this project's C port of Intel's crc32 + pclmulqdq code) and IntelAsm (Intel's original asm).
claimed_speedup: README, 4096-byte buffer, 64-bit i7-4770: SlicingBy8 is 5.1x faster than Sarwate, Hardware64 is 4.2x faster than SlicingBy8, and IntelC is 2.7x faster than Hardware64. Chaining those gives IntelC roughly 58x over the byte-at-a-time Sarwate (derived from page data). On 32-bit Edison, IntelC is 8.8x faster than SlicingBy8. Against the strongest bundled incumbent, Mark Adler's SSE4.2 crc32c, the log-scale chart shows IntelC only modestly ahead (roughly 1.2x on 64-bit i7-4770, read off the chart), and about level with Intel's own asm (IntelAsm), which it is ported from.
compiler_and_flags: g++ 6.3 (i7-4770 32- and 64-bit, Edison) and g++ 7.2 (i7-4770 64-bit, NUC E3815), per the chart labels. crc32c/Makefile uses -O3 -DNDEBUG -flto -msse4.2 -mpclmul, plus -m32/-m64 when CPU_TYPE is set. Intel's crc_iscsi_v_pcl.asm is assembled with yasm. DEBUG=TRUE builds with -g -O0.
hardware: Intel Core i7-4770 (Haswell; 32- and 64-bit builds), Intel Atom E3815 (NUC, 64-bit) and Intel Edison (x86-32 and x86-64), per the chart labels
license: BSD-3-Clause (crc32c/LICENSE, MIT copyright, with Intel slicing-by-8 under the same terms; the README says BSD 2-clause). crc32intelc.cc and crc32adler.cc are under the Zlib license, and crc_iscsi_v_pcl.asm is Intel BSD-3-Clause. GitHub's license API detects none.
tradeoffs: IntelC path is only efficient above 216-byte buffers due to pclmulqdq combine overhead; 32-bit portability path needs inline assembly; unmaintained since 2017
caveats: All the implementations compared are bundled in this repo: evanjones' Sarwate and slicing-by-4/8, Mark Adler's SSE4.2 code, and Intel's asm. The headline ~58x is against byte-at-a-time Sarwate. Against Adler's hardware crc32c the gain is only modest, and IntelC merely matches Intel's own asm, which it ports. The main contribution is portable C that also runs on 32-bit. On 64-bit Edison and the NUC E3815 (Silvermont), the 3-way crc32q+pclmul paths (Adler, IntelC, IntelAsm) are slower than plain Hardware64. The IntelC path only pays off above 216 bytes. It computes CRC-32C (Castagnoli) only, not the zlib/gzip CRC-32. The code is actually C++ (.cc) with inline asm, and the last commit was in 2017.

name: komrad36/CRC ("Golden" hardware-accelerated CRC32)
baseline: The author's own C++/asm reimplementations of bitwise (naive) and slicing-by-1..16 tabular CRC-32C, plus a single-stream SSE4.2 _mm_crc32_u64 loop. zlib is never mentioned or tested.
workload: CRC-32C (Castagnoli poly 0x82F63B78 reflected, the polynomial hard-wired in the x86 SSE4.2 crc32 instruction) of a 900 KB buffer of mt19937 (seed 5) random bytes, repeated 20-10000 runs per option. It compares 13 implementations from bitwise through 16-byte tabular and 1/8-byte hardware crc32 up to 'Golden': 3 parallel SSE4.2 crc32 streams recombined with a PCLMULQDQ carry-less multiply and a LUT of shift constants. There is also a 2-way AMD Jaguar variant.
claimed_speedup: Golden: ~62 bits/cycle vs 8.00 bits/cycle for the 16-byte tabular version (7.75x, derived from page data) and vs 21.30 bits/cycle for a plain 8-byte hardware crc32 loop (~2.9x, derived from page data). The page says naive implementations are 'more than 150x slower than our final Golden result' (0.09-0.33 bits/cycle).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC v142 (Visual Studio 2019), Release x64: /O2 (MaxSpeed), /Oi intrinsics, /arch:AVX2 (per CRC/CRC.vcxproj). The README table does not state which build produced it.
hardware: unspecified "high-end modern x86 CPU"
tradeoffs: Hardware-accelerated "Golden" path requires SSE4.2 (crc32 instruction) plus PCLMULQDQ; earlier tabular options in the same repo are the portable fallback for non-x86/embedded targets.
caveats: This computes CRC-32C (Castagnoli), not the IEEE CRC-32 used by zlib, gzip, PNG and ZIP. The x86 crc32 instruction cannot compute IEEE CRC-32, so it is not a drop-in for zlib crc32(). The README is an educational derivation with a self-reported bits/cycle table on an unnamed 'high-end modern x86 CPU'. main.cpp computes bits/cycle from wall-clock time assuming a 4 GHz clock. The project is a Windows-only MSVC solution and needs SSE4.2 + PCLMULQDQ.

name: ChainHash

claimed_speedup: SMHasher3 Speed at 262,144 bytes: 28.31 B/TSC vs XXH3-64's 19.90 on Xeon 8375C (~1.42x), and 26.26 vs 13.04 B/cycle on Apple M2 Pro (~2.01x) (ratios derived from page data). On short 1-31-byte inputs ChainHash is much slower: 155.14 vs 29.44 cycles/hash on Xeon and 87.49 vs 25.05 on M2.
compiler_and_flags: Xeon: GCC 11.5, SMHasher3 CMake Release build with no global ISA flags (PCLMUL/VPCLMULQDQ/AVX-512 paths chosen at runtime), pinned to CPUs 16-23 with taskset. M2 Pro: Apple Clang 17, -O3 -march=native+crypto -std=c++11 -DNDEBUG (results/64/bench/build_m2.py). SMHasher3 --test=Speed.
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8375C; Apple M2 Pro
tradeoffs: Bulk-only design: short inputs (1-31 bytes) are much slower than XXH3-64 (155 Xeon ticks vs 29 per hash), so it is not a drop-in for small-key hash tables. Also ships a machine-checked (Lean) collision-bound proof and a ChainHash-128 variant; ChainHash-128 loses to XXH3-128 on Xeon (14.43 vs 19.82 B/tick) but wins on M2 Pro (14.43 vs 12.53 B/cycle).
caveats: The author also wrote and ran the benchmark. Raw logs, SHA-256 provenance and the bench scripts are published, but the scripts depend on a separately configured SMHasher3 checkout and are 'archived evidence rather than a runnable distribution'. The Xeon bulk figure is the higher of two passes; M2 figures are medians of three. ChainHash is bulk-only and makes no small-key speed claim: it is ~5x (Xeon) and ~3.5x (M2) slower than XXH3 on 1-31-byte inputs. The repo was created 2026-09-18 and has no independent confirmation yet.

name: HalftimeHash
workload: SMHasher bulk speed test on 256KiB strings on an Intel i7-7800X (Skylake-X, AVX-512), plotted against the fastest SMHasher families (clhash, MeowHash128, xxh128, xxh3, t1ha0_aes_avx2, falkhash). Also benchmark.cpp comparisons against clhash and UMASH on 250KB strings and across input sizes, on the i7-7800X and an AMD EC2 c5a.large (7R32, no AVX-512).
claimed_speedup: SMHasher speed test on 256KiB strings on an i7-7800X, in bytes/cycle from the paper's committed plot data (smhasher-speed.txt): HalftimeHash16 16.942 and HalftimeHash24 15.683 vs xxh128 12.162 and xxh3 12.772. That makes them about 1.39x and 1.29x faster than xxh128 (derived from page data). HalftimeHash32 (13.476) is about 1.11x faster; HalftimeHash40 (9.998) is slower than xxh128. The paper's text says the two fastest variants beat every SMHasher-suite hash on 256KiB strings. Against the AU families clhash and UMASH it claims over 50% higher throughput, exceeding 16 bytes/cycle, and typically 55% faster than clhash on strings over 1KB. On the AMD 7R32 (no AVX-512), HalftimeHash with 256-bit blocks beats clmul-based hashing by up to 2x; the 'up to 2x' figure is stated for AMD only, not for both chips.
compiler_and_flags: Clang++ 11.0.1 on Ubuntu 18.04 (paper). benchmark.cpp (the clhash/UMASH comparison) is built by the repo Makefile with -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -std=c++14 -DNDEBUG. Build flags for the SMHasher run behind the xxh128 comparison (jbapple/smhasher-1, a fork of rurban/smhasher) are not stated.
hardware: Intel i7-7800X (Skylake-X, AVX-512); AMD EC2 c5a.large (7R32, no AVX-512)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++ almost-universal (AU) hash aimed at long-string hashing; wins shown are for 250-256KiB-class strings, not short-key hash-table lookups where xxHash/wyhash are typically used; AU construction needs larger per-instance keyed parameters than a plain xxHash seed.
caveats: The xxh128 comparison comes from one SMHasher speed run on one Intel CPU, with unstated build flags; numbers exist only as plot data (smhasher-speed.txt) behind a figure. Only the two fastest variants (HalftimeHash16/24) clearly beat xxh128; HalftimeHash40 is slower. The AMD 'up to 2x' result is against clhash/UMASH, not xxHash. The default branch has not been committed to since 2022-05-28; the author's only later activity is a 2025-03-08 commit on the non-default 'supercop' branch. Few stars.

name: haya32x64
workload: Pure-JavaScript and wasm one-shot hashing of a 4-byte key and 1 MiB bulk data on AWS EC2 C8a (AMD EPYC 9R45) and C8g (Arm Neoverse V2), Node.js 24.18 / V8 13.6, medians of nine warmed public-API samples, comparing haya32x64 (32-bit-only state/arithmetic) against hayahash64, xxhash-wasm's XXH64, and cyrb53
claimed_speedup: 4-byte one-shot latency with pure-JS haya32x64: 22.9 ns (C8a) and 34.0 ns (C8g), vs xxhash-wasm XXH64 at 39.4 ns and 63.9 ns. That is about 1.7x-1.9x faster (derived from page data). Against the pure-JS xxhashjs XXH64 (1939.3 ns / 2691.0 ns at 4 B; 37 / 28 MB/s at 1 MiB) the gap is far larger. XXH64 via wasm still leads 1 MiB bulk: 15,973 MB/s vs haya32x64's 4,462 MB/s pure-JS and 10,971 MB/s hybrid (C8a). cyrb53 (53-bit output) is faster at 4 B (4.7 ns).
compiler_and_flags: Node.js 24.18.0 / V8 13.6.233.17 on Ubuntu 26.04 for the JS/wasm figures (node --expose-gc bench/js.mjs; xxhash-wasm 1.1.0 and xxhashjs 0.2.2 pinned). Native SMHasher3 built with GCC 15.2.0 -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG.
hardware: AWS EC2 c8a.2xlarge (AMD EPYC 9R45) and c8g.2xlarge (Arm Neoverse V2), timed work pinned to one core
tradeoffs: Restricted to 32-bit state/arithmetic to target pure JS, CSP-restricted/edge runtimes, Cortex-M, RV32 and GLSL; loses on bulk throughput to 64-bit-multiply hashes like XXH64; digest is still labeled experimental and frozen at an interim verification value.
caveats: The win is only for short keys in JavaScript, and xxhash-wasm's latency includes JS-to-wasm call overhead. XXH64 via wasm wins 1 MiB bulk. In native SMHasher3 builds, 64-bit-multiply hashes are much faster: XXH3-64 runs at 60.59 B/cycle vs 7.50 on C8a. haya32x64 beats only 32-bit-arithmetic designs natively, e.g. XXH-32 bulk at 4.89 vs 7.50 B/cycle. name: CLHash
baseline: CityHash (CityHash64WithSeed, the paper's C port of v1.1.1); secondarily xxHash (xxh3) via SMHasher
workload: Paper: hashing random inputs from 8 B to 8 kB (Table 5 reports 64 B and 4 kB), timed with rdtsc over 40 million input words per length, random-bit generation excluded. SMHasher: bulk speed test with 262144-byte keys, run with many hash functions on the same machine and build in rurban/smhasher.
claimed_speedup: Paper Table 5 (i7-4770): 0.16 vs 0.23 cycles/byte for CityHash on 4 kB inputs (authors: 'almost 45% faster'; about 40% faster on inputs over 64 B, similar speed at 32 B or less) and 0.45 vs 0.48 cycles/byte at 64 B. Separately, the rurban SMHasher bulk test (262144-byte keys, Ryzen 5 3350G) gives 22932.36 vs 20853.74 MiB/s for xxh3, about 10% faster (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Paper: GNU GCC 4.8 with -O2 (benchmark code in lemire/StronglyUniversalStringHashing). SMHasher: CMake Release build with -march=native -std=c++11 per rurban/smhasher CMakeLists.txt; compiler version not stated.
hardware: Paper: Intel i7-4770 (Haswell) at 3.4 GHz, 32 GB DDR3-1600, Turbo Boost and hyper-threading disabled. SMHasher: AMD Ryzen 5 3350G 3.6GHz (default table).
stars_or_usage: 302 stars; based on Lemire & Kaser, J. Cryptographic Engineering 6(3), 2016
tradeoffs: Requires PCLMULQDQ+SSE4.2 (x64 Haswell or newer) or ARM PMULL crypto extension; fails to build or is slow on unsupported hardware; CLHASH_BITMIX build flag needed to pass SMHasher's avalanche test.
caveats: The paper-era CLHASH code (StronglyUniversalStringHashing, 2015) is not the current simdhash/clhash library, and the CityHash baseline was the authors' own C port of CityHash 1.1.1 rather than upstream C++. Against xxh3, CLHash wins only on bulk data (about 10% in SMHasher) and is about 2.3x slower on small keys (67.22 vs 29.46 cycles/hash). SMHasher flags a PerlinNoise quality issue, and the paper reports CLHASH fails the SMHasher avalanche test. It is x64 (PCLMULQDQ+SSE4.2) or ARM PMULL only. The README's own claim is '20 to 40x faster' than a naive Java-like polynomial hash, plus about 0.1 cycles/byte on Skylake. The repo was transferred from lemire/clhash (which redirects) to the simdhash org.

name: Rain (Rainbow hash)
baseline: HighwayHash-128 and FarmHash-128.CM (128-bit hashes in the SMHasher3 results table); the repo names no baseline itself
workload: SMHasher3 Speed test as published in the SMHasher3 results README: average cycles/hash over 1-31-byte keys and bulk bytes/cycle at 262144-byte keys, Rainbow 128-bit and 256-bit v3.7.1 against the other hashes that pass all tests. Results page does not name the CPU (harness prints '@ 3.5 ghz').
claimed_speedup: Claim only (README): 'Rainbow is the fastest 128-bit hash, and the fastest 256-bit hash (non-crypto)'; README table gives Rainbow 3-6 GiB/s with no baseline. SMHasher3 results page data: rainbow-128 62.06 cycles on 1-31 byte keys vs HighwayHash-128 99.09 (~1.6x faster, derived from page data), FarmHash-128.CM.seed1 69.61 (~1.1x), MeowHash 61.51 (tie); rainbow-256 103.65 vs HighwayHash-256 154.48 (~1.5x) and PearsonBlock-256 168.68. Not faster elsewhere: rainbow-128 is slower than a5hash-128 (30.27) and MuseAir-128 (30.97) on short keys, and bulk is 1.27 bytes/cycle (4.14 GiB/s at the assumed 3.5 GHz) vs HighwayHash-128 2.87, a5hash-128 6.92, MuseAir-128 7.15 and MeowHash 12.43; rainbow-256 bulk 1.28 vs HighwayHash-256 2.88 and RH512 2.50.
tradeoffs: Rainbow is a roughly 140-line multiply/rotate hash with scalable 64, 128 or 256-bit output that passes all 250 SMHasher3 tests (64-bit variant claimed), but its bulk speed is low (about 1.3 bytes/cycle). The repo also ships Rainstorm, a slower experimental crypto-style hash whose v4 README says an external review found a practical collision for a two-message-round reduction; it is unvetted. WASM port is 4x to 23x slower than the C++ build (README benchmark).
caveats: The README headline claim (fastest 128-bit and 256-bit non-crypto hash) is not supported by the SMHasher3 results page it links: several passing 128-bit hashes (a5hash-128, MuseAir-128, MeowHash) are faster in bulk and on short keys, and at 256 bits HighwayHash-256 and CityHashCrc-256 (which fails some tests) are faster in bulk. The only wins found are narrow (short-key latency against HighwayHash and FarmHash; MeowHash ties). Against the usual non-crypto incumbents it is slower on the same page: 64-bit rainbow is 61.63 cycles and 1.28 bytes/cycle vs XXH-64 52.60 and 3.99, and XXH3-128 (fails some tests) is 36.13 and 12.72. SMHasher3 results list the CPU nowhere; the SMHasher3 README describes the maintainer's machine (AMD Ryzen 9 3950X pinned to 3500 MHz, gcc 9.3) only for its runtime-comparison table, which fits the '@ 3.5 ghz' conversion but is not stated as the results machine. Results come from SMHasher3 20251015, 20251112 or 20260827 release builds. The table is the maintainer's single run; Rain's README licence line credits the SMHasher3 maintainer with improvements to the code, so the suite is not fully arm's length. Results were measured on Rainbow v3.7.1; the 4.0.0 release changed only Rainstorm (README: Rainbow digests unchanged). The repo's own results/smhasher3/rainbow-256-v3.7.1.txt came back as an empty file through raw.githubusercontent.com and was not used. The assigned URL github.com/DOSAYGO-Research/rain resolves to DOSAYGO-STUDIO/rain. [retier] SMHasher3 results (raw/rainbow-128.txt): the README 'fastest 128/256-bit' claim is false on that page; rainbow-128 wins only short-key latency against HighwayHash and FarmHash-128.CM, is about 2x slower bulk than both and slower than XXH-64 and XXH3 on both metrics, and a5hash-128 and MuseAir-128 beat it on both short-key and bulk; RH512 (256-bit, 250/250 pass) beats rainbow-256 on both (79.73 vs 103.65 cycles, 2.50 vs 1.28 B/cycle). No CPU or flags; the SMHasher3 maintainer is credited with code improvements to Rain. The README C++ vs WASM table (4x-23x) times whole process launches (scripts/bench.mjs exec of ./rainsum vs node), one run per row, so rows up to 1 MB are start-up cost and the 100 MB row is about 2.3 vs 1.3 GB/s (about 1.8x, derived). 'link rainbow.o' exports nothing; the Makefile is macOS/Homebrew-only; streaming HashState was broken until 2026-07-27.

name: rustc-hash (FxHash)
baseline: SipHash-1-3 (Rust std DefaultHasher, the default hasher of std::collections::HashMap/HashSet)
workload: Hashing inside rustc's internal hash maps/sets (integers, composite multi-integer keys, short strings/slices), measured as end-to-end rustc compile time on rustc-perf `check` benchmarks
claimed_speedup: Switching rustc's FxHashMap/FxHashSet from FxHasher back to std's DefaultHasher (SipHash-1-3, with the #69152 improvements) regressed every rustc-perf `check` benchmark by 3.9% to 84.7%. Examples: deeply-nested-check avg 63.6% (max 84.7%), syn-check avg 38.7%, helloworld-check avg 23.3%, token-stream-stress-check avg 5.9%. Measured locally in Feb 2020 on the pre-2.0 Firefox-derived FxHash. The Rust Performance Book summarizes this as 'slowdowns ranging from 4-84%'.
stars_or_usage: 597 stars; ~828M all-time crates.io downloads (~225M recent); internal hasher (FxHashMap/FxHashSet) throughout the rustc compiler
tradeoffs: Not DoS-resistant (unsuitable for untrusted-input hash maps, unlike SipHash); current algorithm is a polynomial hash with a wyhash-inspired string compression step, not the original 'FxHash' bit-mix despite the crate keeping that name for compatibility.
caveats: The numbers are first-party end-to-end rustc-perf compile-time results that a rustc/rustc-hash maintainer measured locally in Feb 2020. Hardware, compiler flags and the exact metric are not stated. They cover the old Firefox-derived FxHash. The current 2.x hasher (Orson Peters' polynomial hash with rotation finalizer and wyhash-style string compression) is described only as 'slightly better performance for rustc' in the CHANGELOG, and 2.0 caused a large-hashmap regression in rustc that 2.1.1 mitigated. In the same comment, std HashMap was slightly faster than FxHashMap on an integer-key microbenchmark (fewer collisions). FxHash is not HashDoS-resistant. The repo has no benchmark code (benchmarks PR #50 was closed unmerged).

name: curve25519-voi
baseline: Go standard library crypto/ed25519 and golang.org/x/crypto/curve25519 (X25519) for single operations; ed25519consensus (hdevalence) for batch verification, since stdlib has no batch verify; Cloudflare CIRCL also benchmarked
workload: Ed25519 sign/verify/batch-verify (batch sizes 1-1024) and X25519 scalar multiplication
claimed_speedup: Native (AVX2) build, Go 1.17, i7-10510U. Ed25519 Verify: 125us (stdlib) to 75us, about 1.67x (derived from page data). Sign: 52.7us to 27.5us, about 1.92x (derived from page data). NewKeyFromSeed: 42.8us to 24.3us. X25519 ScalarBaseMult: 107us (x/crypto) to 24us, about 4.5x (derived from page data). X25519 ScalarMult shows no gain (107us vs 106us), and CIRCL is faster there at 65us. Batch verification is measured against ed25519consensus, not stdlib: VerifyBatch_1024 goes from 61.8ms to 31.7ms, about 1.95x (derived from page data), and to 24.0ms with precomputed expanded public keys. With the purego build (no assembly), Verify goes from 181us to 121us and Sign from 73.3us to 50.9us.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.17 toolchain, AMD64 with AVX2 assembly backend enabled; also measured with assembly disabled ("purego")
hardware: Intel Core i7-10510U @ 1.80GHz, turbo disabled
stars_or_usage: 79 stars; oasis-core's go.mod pins curve25519-voi and replaces golang.org/x/crypto/ed25519 and x/crypto/curve25519 with it
tradeoffs: Precomputed public keys cost ~1.47KiB memory each; Go-only, not usable directly from C++; some batch-verify configurations allocate more memory than stdlib
caveats: The batch-verify baseline is ed25519consensus, not Go stdlib, which has no batch verification. X25519 variable-base ScalarMult is no faster than x/crypto, and CIRCL (which uses BMI2) beats it. The benchmark harness for the CIRCL and ed25519consensus comparisons is not in the repo; only the stdlib and x/crypto comparisons are. All numbers come from a single 2021-era laptop CPU on Go 1.17. There is no comparison with OpenSSL or libsodium.
found_via: gh api repos/oasisprotocol/curve25519-voi/contents (repo has a dedicated PERFORMANCE.md; found while surveying Ed25519 performance-focused repos)

verification.tier_reason: PERFORMANCE.md states Go 1.17, Intel Core i7-10510U with turbo disabled, and native (AVX2 assembly) versus purego builds. The stdlib head-to-heads are reproducible from in-repo benchmark code: primitives/ed25519/ed25519_test.go (BenchmarkSigning and BenchmarkVerification, with voi and stdlib sub-benchmarks), primitives/ed25519/batch_verify_test.go and primitives/x25519/x25519_test.go (voi vs x/crypto). Go's gc compiler has no optimisation flags beyond the build tag, so tier A holds.

The record credited the 61.8ms to 31.7ms VerifyBatch_1024 win to stdlib, but that column is ed25519consensus. The record's /blob/main/ benchmark URL returns 404 because the default branch is master. The last commit on master is 2025-11-14, about 10 months ago, so the project is active, not stale.

name: ENG25519 (Curve25519_AVX512IFMA)
baseline: OpenSSL 1.1.1 X25519 (x86-64 assembly, crypto/ec/asm/x25519-x86_64.pl) and Ed25519 (C implementation, crypto/ec/curve25519.c), extracted from OpenSSL_1_1_1-stable and compiled into the paper's benchmark harness; the TLS-level experiments use OpenSSL 1.1.1q
workload: Warm-start CPU-cycle cost (2,000 warm-up runs, average of 20,000 runs) of X25519-KeyGen, Ed25519-Sign/Verify and fixed-point scalar multiplication on an Intel Xeon Ice Lake server. Only X25519-KeyGen is batched (8x1-way: eight keypairs per call). Ed25519-Sign (1x8-way) and Ed25519-Verify (1x2-way) run one operation per call and use AVX-512IFMA lanes internally. OpenSSL runs one operation at a time on scalar x86-64 code
claimed_speedup: X25519-KeyGen 12.01x, Ed25519-Sign 3.79x, Ed25519-Verify 3.33x, fixed-point scalar multiplication 8.06x higher throughput than OpenSSL (paper Tables 2-4)
compiler_and_flags: GCC 9.2.0, -O2 (artifact CMake Release flags: -mavx512ifma -O2 -funroll-loops -m64 -march=native -mtune=native -fomit-frame-pointer -fwrapv); OpenSSL code extracted and built with the same options
hardware: Intel Xeon (Ice Lake) Platinum 8369B, 8 vCPUs, Alibaba Cloud ecs.c7.2xlarge (Turbo Boost left enabled)
tradeoffs: Speedups are for N-way batched operations (8x/2x parallel instances) vs OpenSSL's 1-way scalar calls, not single-call latency; requires AVX-512IFMA hardware (Ice Lake or newer); deployed via a custom OpenSSL ENGINE, not a drop-in library
caveats: The 12.01x X25519-KeyGen ratio compares an 8-keypair batched call (60,479 cycles per 8 keys) with OpenSSL generating one keypair per call, so it measures throughput rather than single-operation latency. The Ed25519 ratios (3.79x and 3.33x) are per operation. The OpenSSL baseline is OpenSSL 1.1.1 code extracted and recompiled inside the authors' harness, not a stock or current OpenSSL build. Turbo Boost was left enabled (the authors argue it causes no significant jitter). The code needs an AVX-512IFMA CPU. End-to-end, the paper reports 25% and 35% more TLS 1.3 handshakes per second than the stock OpenSSL X25519 and P-256 configurations (1,707 vs 1,366 and 1,260 connections per second), far below the micro-benchmark ratios.
found_via: GitHub graphql search: 'ed25519 avx512 fast in:name,description,readme'

verification.tier_reason: USENIX Security 2024 paper Tables 2-4 compare directly against OpenSSL 1.1.1 X25519/Ed25519 with GCC 9.2.0, -O2 and Xeon Platinum 8369B stated; the benchmark code (Crypto/Curve25519_AVX512IFMA/test.c, with OpenSSL's x86-64 asm and C code vendored in src/openssl_curve25519.*) is public in the artifact repo, so tier A stands.
verification.notes: All claimed ratios appear exactly in the paper: 12.01 (Table 2), 3.79 and 3.33 (Table 3), 8.06 (Table 4). The only fix needed was the workload: the record said Ed25519-Sign was 8-way batched, but it is a 1x8-way single-signature implementation. Metadata checks out: LGPL-3.0, 14 stars, last commit 2024-06-12 (stale), not archived, not a fork.

corrected_fields.workload: Warm-start CPU-cycle throughput of X25519 KeyGen/Derive and Ed25519 Sign/Verify, using 8-way (X25519-KeyGen, Ed25519-Sign) / 2-way (Ed25519-Verify) AVX-512IFMA batching vs OpenSSL's 1-way scalar x86-64 asm, on an Intel Xeon Ice Lake server

name: Falcon-Mitaka GPU (High Throughput Lattice-based Signatures on GPUs)
baseline: Falcon NIST-submission AVX2-optimized CPU implementation (Fouque et al. [4]); Mitaka is compared only against its FP64 reference C. liboqs was not benchmarked.
workload: Falcon-512/1024 batched signing and verification throughput on GPU (K up to 16,384 signatures per launch) vs the Falcon AVX2-optimized CPU implementation; Mitaka-512/1024 GPU vs the Mitaka FP64 reference C
claimed_speedup: The paper's stated ratios do not match its own tables. '7.78x sign / 52.43x verify vs AVX2' (RTX 3080, Falcon-512) is actually vs the FP64 reference (27908/3587, 1913380/36491). 'Falcon-1024 20.56x/148.56x' equals A100 Falcon-512 throughput divided by AVX2 Falcon-1024 throughput. The abstract's '20.03x/29.51x' equals Mitaka-512 on A100 vs the Mitaka FP64 reference. Recomputed from Tables 5/6, Falcon GPU batch throughput (K=16384) vs AVX2 CPU (derived from page data): Falcon-512 RTX 3080 8.81x sign / 104.96x verify; Falcon-1024 RTX 3080 5.35x / 66.45x; Falcon-512 A100 18.50x / 149.29x; Falcon-1024 A100 13.18x / 114.24x.
compiler_and_flags: GPU: CUDA 11 (paper Table 4); repo Makefile uses CUDA 11.7 nvcc -rdc=true -arch sm_86 with gcc as the host compiler. Compiler/flags for the CPU AVX2 baseline are not stated anywhere in the paper.
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3080 (8704 CUDA cores; desktop host Intel i9-10900K @3.70GHz) plus A100/V100/T4 on the ARDC Nectar cloud (host Intel Xeon Gold 6150 @2.2GHz). The paper does not say which CPU or how many threads produced the AVX2/FP64 CPU baseline rates in Table 6.
tradeoffs: Needs a CUDA GPU and large signature batches to amortize kernel-launch overhead; single-signature latency is not necessarily better than CPU; public repo only ships Falcon-512 and Mitaka-512, not the 1024 variants benchmarked in the paper.
caveats: This compares a GPU batch against a CPU implementation of unstated thread count, so the >50x verify ratios are a hardware and batching effect. Per-batch latency is high (e.g. 587 ms for a 16,384-signature Falcon-512 sign batch on the RTX 3080). The paper's own speedup text misattributes baselines (see claimed_speedup). Released code covers only Falcon-512 and Mitaka-512, targets sm_86, and has no CPU baseline harness. It rebuilds the LDL tree on every signature. No commits since 2023-11-14.
found_via: IACR ePrint search "GPU signature verification throughput" -> eprint.iacr.org/2023/399; repo link found inside the paper PDF text ("We open-sourced our implementation to https://github.com/benlwk/Falcon-Mitaka")

verification.tier_reason: The paper is peer-reviewed (IEEE TPDS 2024, DOI 10.1109/TPDS.2024.3367319) and its Table 6 compares GPU throughput against the Falcon AVX2 CPU implementation, so B. It is not A because the paper gives no compiler, flags, thread count or even which CPU ran the AVX2 baseline (Table 4 lists only 'CUDA 11'). The repo has no AVX2 baseline harness, and its released code covers only Falcon-512 and Mitaka-512.
verification.notes: The main fix is claimed_speedup: none of the record's three headline ratio pairs is actually Falcon-vs-AVX2 per the paper's own Tables 5/6, so I replaced them with ratios recomputed from the page data. Metadata (GPL-3.0, 5 stars, last commit 2023-11-14, stale, copyable) checks out.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Falcon-512 on RTX 3080: 7.78x sign / 52.43x verify faster than AVX2 CPU; Falcon-1024: 20.56x sign / 148.56x verify faster than AVX2 CPU (Table 6); on A100, 20.03x/29.51x vs AVX2 (abstract)

name: fasthqc/hqc (vectorized sparse-dense multiplication + syndrome generation)
baseline: HQC NIST Round 2 optimized reference implementation (Aguilar-Melchior et al.); HQC is a KEM historically supported by liboqs
workload: Clock-cycle counts for HQC Round-2 keygen, encryption and decryption (KEM) across all six Round-2 parameter sets (N = 24677 to 70853). Each figure is the average over 50 random data sets of the minimum of 1,000 runs, after 1,000 warm-up runs. The report also micro-benchmarks sparse-dense polynomial multiplication and syndrome_gen.
claimed_speedup: The report states "about 34 to 46%" fewer clock cycles than the HQC Round-2 optimized implementation with both patches applied. On the i5-4690S (Table 4): keygen 34.9-42.8%, encryption 33.7-45.2%, decryption 45.0-46.3%. On the i5-8400H (Table 8): keygen 32.5-36.3%, encryption 30.9-37.9%, decryption 40.0-43.2%. As speed ratios this is about 1.45-1.86x (derived from page data). The vectorized sparse-dense multiplication alone is "about 70-75%" faster (Table 1). syndrome_gen drops from 400,209 to 18,101 cycles, about 22x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 7.4.0 (Ubuntu 7.4.0-1ubuntu1~18.04.1), stated only for the i5-8400H (patch v3) runs; no compiler is stated for the i5-4690S runs. Flags from Fast_Implementation/hqc-256-3/Makefile: -O3 -std=c99 -mavx -mavx2. Turbo Boost disabled.
hardware: Intel Core i5-4690S @ 3.20GHz (4th gen); Intel Core i5-8400H @ 2.50GHz (8th gen)
tradeoffs: No LICENSE file present (code can be studied/reimplemented but not safely reused/redistributed); targets HQC Round-2 parameter sets, which predate HQC's later NIST selection and parameter revisions, so exact percentages may not transfer to the current spec
caveats: The report and code predate HQC's selection for NIST standardization and its later parameter and spec changes, and the project has been abandoned since 2020. The repo has no license. The public patched harness under Fast_Implementation covers only hqc-256-3; the README says the implementation 'moved to ARITH2020', and that folder holds per-table experiments. The report does not state whether the patched code is constant-time; the repo's ARITH2020/TABLE4 also ships a randomized FastConvolution variant. liboqs disabled HQC by default in 0.13.0 (April 2025) over a reported security flaw. It re-enabled HQC by default in 0.16.0 (July 2026) using the updated 20250822-spec implementation. None of this concerns this specific patch.
found_via: GitHub graphql search: 'hqc post-quantum fast avx2 in:name,description,readme'

verification.tier_reason: The report compares the patch against the HQC Round-2 optimized implementation. For the i5-8400H runs it states gcc 7.4.0. The benchmark code (Fast_Implementation/hqc-256-3/src/main_hqc.c plus script.sh, which runs the code without and then with the patch) is public, and the Makefile gives CFLAGS -O3 -std=c99 -mavx -mavx2, so tier A holds. It holds only narrowly: the headline i5-4690S numbers state no compiler, and the public harness covers only hqc-256-3.
verification.notes: The numbers are on the page, but the record's '35.1-46.3%' range was misstated: the true minimum on the i5-4690S is 33.7% (encryption, N = 24677), and the i5-8400H results (30.9-43.2%) were left out. The liboqs caveat was out of date (HQC is now re-enabled). The repo describes the code as the 'Arith 27 conference submission 16', but crossref turned up no published ARITH 2020 paper, so none is claimed.

corrected_fields.workload: HQC key-encapsulation cycle counts (sparse-dense polynomial multiplication and syndrome generation) across HQC-128/192/256 parameter sets

name: libsecp256k1 (bitcoin-core/secp256k1)
workload: ECDSA signature verification (parse compressed pubkey, parse DER signature, verify) on the secp256k1 curve, benchmarked via dlopen loading of historical OpenSSL and libsecp256k1 release versions on the same binary
claimed_speedup: ECDSA verify on secp256k1 (compressed-pubkey parse + DER sig parse + verify), libsecp256k1 at Bitcoin Core v30.0 (v0.7.0, commit b9313c6) vs OpenSSL 3.5.0. Ryzen 9 5950X (Wuille): 8.5x (stated). Author's arm64 with gcc 14.2.0: '>8x' stated, about 8.3x read from the chart. Ryzen 9 3950X with gcc 12.2.0 (independent issue #2): about 9.0x read from the chart. Historical baseline, libsecp at Core v0.12 (2015) vs OpenSSL 1.1.1: about 4.3x (arm64), 5.4x (5950X) and 4.8x (3950X), read from the charts. The original PR #6954 claim was 2.5-5.5x. Chart readings are pixel measurements, accurate to about ±2-3%.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler: gcc 14.2.0 for the author's arm64 run and gcc 12.2.0 for the independent 3950X run. Wuille's 5950X run does not state a compiler. All builds use defaults with no custom flags. libsecp256k1 was built with ./autogen.sh && ./configure --enable-static=no --enable-benchmark=no --enable-tests=no --enable-exhaustive-tests=no && make, which gives autoconf '-g -O2' plus libsecp's own -O2 (checked in the v0.7.0 configure.ac). OpenSSL was built with ./config shared && make, whose Linux release default is -O3 (checked in 3.5.0 Configurations/10-main.conf). The harness itself is built with plain cc. These are not Bitcoin Core's own build flags.
hardware: Author: unnamed arm64 machine (he says 3 machines gave very similar results). Wuille: AMD Ryzen 9 5950X. Independent: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X, 32GB RAM, Debian x86_64.
stars_or_usage: 2.5k stars; consensus-critical ECDSA/Schnorr library in Bitcoin Core since 2015, also used by Ethereum, libp2p, and most cryptocurrency software
tradeoffs: Narrow scope (secp256k1 only) vs. OpenSSL's general-purpose EC support; requires a separate dependency instead of reusing an existing OpenSSL install
caveats: Speedup figures are first-party, from Bitcoin Core developers (who also wrote libsecp256k1), in a 2015 PR and in release notes. They have no published benchmark harness, compiler or flags, and they compare against 2015-era OpenSSL, not a current OpenSSL. Figures cover verification only. Signing moved to libsecp256k1 in v0.10.0 mainly for constant-time and side-channel reasons, not measured speed. The repo's bench binaries (README Benchmark section) time libsecp256k1 alone and do not compare against OpenSSL. The IBD/reindex timings are whole-node measurements that include non-crypto work. [retier] The two headline runs (>8x and 8.5x) are first-party: both are listed in libsecp256k1 SECURITY.md. The only independent run is a GitHub issue with a chart and no stated ratio. OpenSSL's secp256k1 path is not specially optimized (the post notes P-256 is heavily optimized, and OpenSSL PR #26097 aims to speed up secp256k1), so this comparison does not show OpenSSL is slow in general. The harness uses the deprecated EC_KEY/o2i_ECPublicKey/ECDSA_verify API. Each run times the 5000 signatures once by default; Wuille used 500000 iterations because of run-to-run variance. OpenSSL 0.9.8h and 1.0.0 crash on arm64 and were skipped. Old libsecp versions were built with modern compilers, which biases the history (Wuille). Arch-dependent: bc-22.0 safegcd gave about 30% on arm64, -3.6% on the 5950X and about 16% on the 3950X, and bc-27.0 (x86_64 asm removal) gave +8% on the 5950X. The harness repo has no license. The archive file is on branch 'master', not 'main'.
found_via: GitHub code search: "faster than OpenSSL" ECDSA -> jamesob/delving-bitcoin-archive (mirror of a Nov 2025 delvingbitcoin.org forum post by theStack), reproducible via github.com/theStack/secp256k1-plugbench
GitHub search 'faster than OpenSSL ecdsa' variants and direct lookup of bitcoin-core/secp256k1; HN Algolia query 'libsecp256k1 openssl' surfacing the r/Bitcoin discussion of the 0.10.0 release notes

verification.tier_reason: Upgraded from D. Bitcoin Core PR #6954, which switched validation from OpenSSL to libsecp256k1, gives first-party numbers: signature validation is 2.5-5.5x faster. The v0.12.0 release notes say validation is over 5x faster on x86_64, and reindex/new-block validation takes less than half the time. No compiler, flags or benchmark harness is stated for the micro figures, so this cannot be A or B.
verification.notes: The record said no numbers existed, but PR #6954 and the v0.12.0 release notes give quantified wins over OpenSSL, so the tier goes D to C and the verdict is confirm. Metadata checked via gh: MIT license, not a fork, not archived, 2,484 stars, last commit 2026-09-25, active; all match the record.

retier.reason: Upgraded from C. Source is Delving Bitcoin topic 2087 (Nov 2025) by Sebastian Falbesoner (theStack). It uses a public harness, github.com/theStack/secp256k1-plugbench. build_libs.sh pins the exact libsecp256k1 commits used in Bitcoin Core v0.12 through v30.0 and the OpenSSL tags 0.9.8h, 1.0.0, 1.1.1, 3.0.0, 3.1.0, 3.3.0 and 3.5.0, all as default shared builds. secp-plugbench.c dlopens each .so and times, with CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID, pubkey parse + DER signature parse + ECDSA verify over 5000 signatures made with libsecp256k1. The OpenSSL path uses EC_GROUP_precompute_mult. Three runs have results. (1) The author on an arm64 machine with gcc 14.2.0 reports >8x (first-party). (2) Pieter Wuille on a Ryzen 5950X with 500000 iterations reports 8.5x (first-party; compiler not stated). (3) Bayernatoor, an independent third party with 0 commits in bitcoin-core/secp256k1, reproduced it in plugbench issue #2 on an AMD Ryzen 9 3950X with gcc 12.2.0 on Debian x86_64 (chart only, about 9.0x). Falbesoner and Wuille are both listed in secp256k1 SECURITY.md (maintainer keys), so they are first-party. The A criteria are met: public code, a stated compiler, default flags fixed by the public build script, and a stated CPU. Run 3 meets all of them and is independent. Run 1 lacks only the CPU model.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: more than 8x faster than OpenSSL's latest release for ECDSA verify (8.5x measured on an AMD Ryzen 5950X, similar ratio on arm64); libsecp256k1 was 2.5-5.5x faster at Bitcoin Core's 2015 switchover from OpenSSL
corrected_fields.hardware: arm64 machine (primary run, 3 machines total tested); independently reproduced by libsecp256k1 author Pieter Wuille on an AMD Ryzen 5950X, 500000 iterations
corrected_fields.caveats: Benchmark measures libsecp256k1 built with defaults, not necessarily Bitcoin Core's exact compile flags; author notes OpenSSL has heavily optimized secp256r1 (unlike secp256k1), so the gap is curve-specific, not a general OpenSSL weakness. Older, less rigorous claims of similar magnitude corroborate via the same underlying library: ofek/coincurve's docs ("more than 10x faster than OpenSSL") and piotrnar/gocoin's 2013 changelog ("sipasec cgo ... over 5 times faster than openssl" for EC_Verify).
corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: gcc 14.2.0; default shared-library builds (`./config shared && make` for OpenSSL, default build for libsecp256k1), no special CFLAGS

name: moduletto (NEON i16 ML-KEM-512)
baseline: liboqs 0.16.0 (ML-KEM-512, built from source at tag 0.16.0, Release, -O3 -march=native, on aarch64/Apple M5)
workload: Full ML-KEM-512 KEM session (keygen+encaps+decaps), 10,000 iterations/100-iteration warmup, ACVP FIPS 203 conformant, on Apple M5 NEON
claimed_speedup: ~1.18x faster full ML-KEM-512 session than LibOQS 0.16.0: 13.7-14.1 us vs 16.19 us per session. The page lists moduletto at 0.85x of LibOQS time; the README says ~1.18x. That is ~72,000 vs 61,800 sessions/sec, and moduletto is faster in all three phases: keygen 4.07 vs 4.72 us, encaps 3.84 vs 5.25 us, decaps 5.80 vs 6.22 us. Against the Kyber C reference (47.87 us, carried over from an unre-measured 2026-03-19 run) it is ~3.4-3.5x faster (derived from page data). The page's 2.96x is Kyber-ref vs LibOQS 0.16.0, not vs moduletto.
compiler_and_flags: moduletto: rustc (version unstated), Cargo release profile opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1, panic=abort; sha3 0.10 with the asm feature; timed by examples/kyber_benchmark (10,000 iterations, 100-iteration warmup). LibOQS: cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DOQS_MINIMAL_BUILD=KEM_ml_kem_512 -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="-O3 -march=native" from tag 0.16.0, C compiler not named; a source comment says gcc. The LibOQS harness is not published and its results are hardcoded in the example.
hardware: Apple M5 (Mac17,2), macOS Darwin 25.5.0
tradeoffs: NEON-only fast path (i64 NTT + SHA3/inline-Keccak backends are 2.5-3x slower fallbacks for non-ARM); single-developer project, no independent security review; author's own doc flags that fixing FIPS 203 conformance bugs (found via ACVP vectors) was what got it under LibOQS, not the SIMD work alone
caveats: The margin over LibOQS is small (1.18x), and the author notes LibOQS 0.16.0 is itself 1.26x faster than 0.15.0, so comparisons against older releases overstate the lead. The LibOQS and Kyber-C-reference numbers are hardcoded constants in examples/kyber_benchmark.rs, measured by an unpublished C harness; the Kyber-ref column comes from a 2026-03-19 session and was not re-measured. The ML-KEM-512 KEM itself lives in the benchmark example, not the library API: the crate provides modular arithmetic and NTT. It only became FIPS 203 conformant on 2026-08-11, after ACVP vectors exposed six deviations, including a hardcoded zero implicit-rejection seed. The Platform Notes section at the bottom of BENCHMARKS.md is stale: it describes 2026-03-19, LibOQS 0.15.0 and Apple clang 17. name: Optimizing Dilithium Implementation with AVX2/AVX-512 (PSPM)
baseline: pq-crystals/dilithium AVX2 implementation: the 'standard' branch (FIPS 204 ML-DSA) AVX2 code for the headline Table XI numbers, and the NIST Round 3 submission AVX2 code for Table IX. This is the upstream code that liboqs/PQClean also derive from; liboqs and PQClean were not benchmarked directly.
workload: Round 3 Dilithium2/3/5 and FIPS 204 ML-DSA-44/65/87 KeyGen, Sign and Verify cycle counts on one core (median of 100000 runs). PSPM(-TEE) replaces NTT for the small-polynomial products (c·s, c·e) in both the AVX2 and AVX-512 implementations, not only on the AVX-512 path. Metric is per-operation cycles (latency).
claimed_speedup: Cycle-count reductions of AVX-512 vs the pq-crystals FIPS 204 AVX2 code (Table XI) for ML-DSA-44/65/87: KeyGen 43.2%/39.3%/45.6%, Sign 36.6%/41.6%/43.7%, Verify 45.3%/46.5%/47.4%. For example, ML-DSA-44 KeyGen drops from 84270 to 47760 cycles. That is about 1.58x-1.90x faster (derived from page data). Against the NIST Round 3 AVX2 code (Table IX), Dilithium2/3/5 cycle reductions are 50.0%-65.1%, about 2.0x-2.9x (derived from page data). Within both the AVX2 and the AVX-512 implementations, PSPM cuts c·s / c·e multiplication cycles by 47%-66% versus NTT (Table VI, Dilithium3).
compiler_and_flags: gcc-9.4.0 with -Wshadow -Wpointer-arith -mavx2 -mavx512f -mavx512vbmi -mavx512bw -mavx512cd -mavx512vl -mpopcnt -maes -march=native -mtune=native -O3. The paper prints the AVX-512 flags as '-mAVX-512F' etc.; the repo Makefiles use -mavx512*.
hardware: Intel Core i7-11700F (Rocket Lake) at 2.5 GHz, TurboBoost and Hyper-Threading disabled, Ubuntu 20.04
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512 hardware support (not present on all deployed x86-64 CPUs, and historically disabled on some consumer Intel chips); the PSPM technique changes the internal multiplication algorithm, so it is not a drop-in replacement without re-verifying constant-time behavior.
caveats: The repo has no LICENSE file (GitHub license null), so it is reference-only. The code derives from the NIST reference Dilithium and PQClean, but the repo itself grants no license. The repo describes itself as 'the source code of the paper Optimizing Dilithium Implementation with AVX2/-512', but the arXiv v3 PDF still says 'We will later open source our code' and does not link it. The owner xurq5953 does not match a listed author name, so the attribution rests on the repo's own statement. The repo holds Round 3 Dilithium only (Dilithium2 sk 2528 bytes), so the headline ML-DSA numbers in the abstract/Table XI cannot be reproduced from it. The percentages are cycle reductions, not throughput increases. The paper says the implementation is not fully constant-time-audited. It also notes that some hash functions are not yet vectorized.

name: UltrafastSecp256k1
baseline: OpenSSL (ECDSA_do_sign/ECDSA_do_verify, secp256k1); also benchmarked against libsecp256k1 (bitcoin-core)
workload: Single-operation ECDSA sign/verify and Schnorr (BIP-340) sign/verify on secp256k1, via the project's bench_unified microbenchmark (RDTSCP timer, 11 passes, 500-iteration warmup, pinned core, turbo disabled)
claimed_speedup: Versus OpenSSL ECDSA_do_sign/ECDSA_do_verify on secp256k1: ECDSA sign 21.56x and verify 10.89x faster (FAST path), 21.70x for constant-time signing, and generator multiplication 44.53x (ratios printed on the page). Versus the in-tree libsecp256k1 (derived from page data): constant-time ECDSA sign about 1.52x (29,406.82 vs 19,311.25 ns), constant-time Schnorr sign about 1.48x (22,544.75 vs 15,232.60 ns), ECDSA verify about 1.13x (41,501.75 vs 36,772.26 ns) and Schnorr verify about 1.15x (42,088.13 vs 36,754.89 ns). The 19,441.6 ns figure the record labeled CT-vs-CT is actually the non-CT FAST sign. In Bitcoin Core bench_bitcoin ConnectBlock runs (README and docs/BITCOIN_CORE_BENCH_RESULTS.json, measured 2026-05-12, not this page) the gain is +0.9-1.5% with LTO and -0.5 to -1.0% without LTO.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2.0, Release+LTO, -O3 -flto -march=native (libsecp256k1 comparison compiled -O3 -march=native, no LTO, in the same binary)
hardware: Intel Core i5-14400F; governor=performance, intel_pstate/no_turbo=1, pinned to core 0 via taskset, TSC 2.496GHz
stars_or_usage: 55 stars; Bitcoin Core PR #35469 (opt-in secondary secp256k1 backend) was closed unmerged with a Concept NACK on 2026-06-05
tradeoffs: The large margin over OpenSSL mostly reflects OpenSSL's unoptimized generic EC code path for secp256k1 (a curve OpenSSL does not special-case the way it does NIST P-curves), so it is a much easier target than the curve's actual production incumbent, libsecp256k1; against libsecp256k1 the realistic block-validation workload shows near-parity
caveats: The benchmark is first-party and self-reported, with no third-party reproduction. The JSON does not record the OpenSSL version (system library). OpenSSL uses its generic prime-curve code for secp256k1, so the >10x OpenSSL ratios reflect a weak baseline; the relevant incumbent, libsecp256k1, is beaten by only about 1.1-1.5x in micro-benchmarks. In those comparisons libsecp256k1 was compiled without LTO while Ultra used LTO. The ConnectBlock gain is about 1% and needs LTO; without LTO it turns negative. That benchmark also reuses only 5 pubkeys, which the repo itself says inflates the ECDSA-verify share of the gain through caching. The repo's metadata admits an earlier benchmark file mislabeled the libsecp256k1 version (the actual version is a pre-v0.8.0 master snapshot, f9a944f). No external security audit exists; all audit evidence is self-generated. Bitcoin Core rejected the backend PR (#35469, Concept NACK, citing its human-review bar). [retier] Benchmark build used experimental REPSEARCH_* flags absent from public sources; Sep 2026 correctness fixes (#400 batch verify accepted invalid signatures, #401 Pippenger, #402 sqrt) postdate the numbers; OpenSSL version not recorded.

name: VecFalcon (Vectorized Falcon-Sign)
baseline: C-FN-DSA (Thomas Pornin's FN-DSA/Falcon implementation, github.com/pornin/c-fn-dsa at commit 96e3b92), SHAKE256X4 variant
workload: Falcon-512/1024 sign_core (SHAKE256X4 PRNG variant; SHAKE256X8 on AVX-512F) CPU-cycle medians over 10,000 runs (x86, ARM) or 2,000 runs (RISC-V) across SSE2, AVX2, AVX-512F, NEON, RV64GC, RV64GCB, RV64GCV and RV64GCVB. Also micro-benchmarks of the vectorized BaseSampler and the RVV/RV64D FFT/iFFT.
claimed_speedup: Falcon-512 sign_core cycles vs the C-FN-DSA reference: 1.13x SSE2, 1.23x AVX2, 1.36x AVX-512F, 1.17x NEON, 1.37x RV64GC, 1.36x RV64GCB, 1.58x RV64GCV, 1.59x RV64GCVB (the paper reports these as 13-59% improvements). Falcon-1024: 1.14x-1.59x. The BaseSampler core without PRNG is 4.2x (SSE2), 8.4x (AVX2), 9.8x (AVX-512F), 7.7x (RVV), 3.8x (RV64IM) and 1.8x (NEON) faster than the C-FN-DSA ref core. With PRNG included it is 1.3x-2.7x. RVV FFT/iFFT is 4.1x-4.7x faster than ref on the SpacemiT X60, and RV64D FFT/iFFT is 2.7x-3.0x faster.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3.0 (x86-64, Ubuntu 24.04); Clang 10.0.0 (ARM, Ubuntu 20.04); GCC 13.2.0 (RISC-V, Bianbu 1.0.15). All builds use -O2 -DFNDSA_SHAKE256X4=1. x86 builds pin the ISA with -msse2, -mavx2 or -mavx512f plus -mno-* flags for higher extensions. RISC-V builds use -march=rv64gc, rv64gc_zba_zbb, rv64gcv or rv64gcv_zba_zbb.
hardware: Intel i7-11700K (Rocket Lake, 3.6GHz, Turbo Boost and Hyper-Threading disabled); ARM Cortex-A72 (Raspberry Pi 4B, 1.5GHz); SpacemiT X60, RVV v1.0 VLEN=256 (Milk-V Jupiter, 2.0GHz)
license: MIT (root LICENSE). The C-FN-DSA-derived opt/ and ref/ directories carry the Unlicense. opt/fft_neon.c is Apache-2.0 (derived from GMUCERG Falcon_NEON).

tradeoffs: Baseline is the C-FN-DSA reference implementation, not liboqs's own bundled Falcon backend directly, though the two are architecturally related (liboqs's Falcon derives from the same lineage of reference/optimized code); the vectorized BaseSampler deliberately breaks bit-for-bit KAT reproducibility with official test vectors while preserving verification interoperability
caveats: Gains are for signature generation (sign_core) only, not keygen or verify, and are measured on the SHAKE256X4 variant, which is not KAT-compatible with default Falcon signing (interoperable for verification). Part of the gain comes from integrated third-party code: XKCP 8-way Keccak on AVX-512F; the BK22 hybrid Keccak and NG23 NEON FFT on ARM; ZYHK25 Keccak on RISC-V. The paper measured C-FN-DSA as faster than the NIST-submission AVX2 code on the i7-11700K, so it is a strong baseline. The only direct comparison with other optimized prior work is at the BaseSampler level (NG23 NEON is slower than ref). Licensing is mixed: MIT, Unlicense (public-domain dedication, no patent grant) and Apache-2.0 files. GitHub's detector reports NOASSERTION.

name: Ed25519 (original amd64-64-24k SUPERCOP/eBATS submission)
baseline: OpenSSL ECDSA (NIST P-256), benchmarked as SUPERCOP/eBATS entry 'ecdonaldp256' (an OpenSSL-based ECDSA wrapper)
workload: Single-signature signing and verification (and batch verification of 64 signatures) on an Intel Xeon E5620 Westmere core (machine 'hydra2'), measured in CPU cycles via the eBATS benchmarking framework
claimed_speedup: Signing: 87548 cycles vs ecdonaldp256 (OpenSSL-based ECDSA P-256) at 1790936 cycles, ~20.5x faster (derived from page data). Single-signature verification: 273364 vs 2087500 cycles, ~7.6x faster (derived from page data). Batch verification of 64 signatures takes 8.55 million cycles (under 134000 cycles/signature), ~15.6x faster than ecdonaldp256 verification (derived from page data). All figures are on hydra2 (Xeon E5620, Westmere).
hardware: Intel Xeon E5620 (Westmere, 2.4 GHz), eBATS machine 'hydra2', Turbo Boost disabled
stars_or_usage: Foundational EdDSA implementation; later adopted (with modifications) by libsodium, OpenSSH, OpenSSL 1.1+, GnuPG, Signal, and most modern TLS stacks
tradeoffs: Ed25519 uses a fixed, non-NIST curve and deterministic nonces, which differ from ECDSA's API/semantics and key format; this original submission is unpadded raw assembly (amd64-64-24k), not a general-purpose library API.
caveats: The paper does not say ecdonaldp256 uses OpenSSL; it only says 'ECDSA signatures using the NIST P-256 elliptic curve'. The OpenSSL basis is confirmed by current eBATS, which lists ecdonaldp256 implementations 'openssl' and 'opensslnew' (code calls EC_KEY_new). The paper does not state compiler or flags. The hydra2 figures come from the radix-2^51 / 30KB-table code that the paper targets at Westmere (i.e. amd64-51-30k, inferred from Sections 3-4), not the radix-2^64 amd64-64-24k variant, which the paper says bottlenecks on Nehalem/Westmere. The numbers are 2011-era; the implementations still ship in SUPERCOP and are still benchmarked on eBATS alongside the newer lib25519 code. The software is a public-domain dedication with no patent grant; the authors say they have not been notified of any patent claims.

name: FourQlib (SchnorrQ / FourQ curve arithmetic)
baseline: NIST P-256 (Gueron-Krasnov fast implementation, the code later merged into OpenSSL as nistz256)
workload: Variable-base and fixed-base elliptic-curve scalar multiplication (the core operation underlying ECDH and SchnorrQ signing/verification), modeled as one ephemeral Diffie-Hellman round, on several x64 CPUs
claimed_speedup: Table 5 (ePrint 2015/565): variable-base scalar multiplication up to 5.6x faster than the Gueron-Krasnov P-256 implementation [27] (Sandy Bridge 72k vs 400k cycles; Haswell 56k vs 312k). One ephemeral DH round is up to 4.4x faster than P-256 (Sandy Bridge 112k vs 490k). Variable-base is 2.2-2.9x faster than the Curve25519 implementations [3,14], and ephemeral DH 1.9-3.7x faster.
hardware: Intel Atom N570 (1.66GHz), Core i7-2600 Sandy Bridge (3.4GHz), Core i7-3770 Ivy Bridge (3.4GHz), Core i7-4770 Haswell (3.4GHz), Core i5-5300U Broadwell (2.30GHz), AMD A8 PRO-7600B Kaveri (3.1GHz); TurboBoost/TurboCore disabled
tradeoffs: FourQ is a non-NIST, non-standardized curve, so adopting it trades interoperability/standard compliance for speed; correct use requires careful handling of the curve's cofactor and endomorphisms for security.
caveats: The P-256 comparison figures (Sandy Bridge and Haswell only) were copied directly from the Gueron-Krasnov paper [27], not re-measured on the FourQ authors' machines. That code is the basis of OpenSSL's ecp_nistz256, whose header credits Gueron and Krasnov. The paper states no compiler or flags, only CPU models. The benchmark CPUs are 2011-2015-era. No SchnorrQ signing/verification cycle comparison against a baseline appears in the paper, which covers scalar multiplication and DH only. The core is MIT-licensed, but the ARM folders include CC0 wrappers and LGPL-3.0 libopencm3.

name: Code Generation of Faster Formally Verified NTT with Plantard Reduction
baseline: NIST PQC / pq-crystals reference C implementations of ML-KEM (Kyber ref) and ML-DSA (Dilithium ref) for end-to-end and NTT results, plus formosa-mlkem Jasmin (NTT only); mlkem-native/mldsa-native scalar C (OPT=0 AUTO=0) is compared only at NTT level
workload: ML-KEM-512 decapsulation/encapsulation/keygen and ML-DSA-2 signing/verification/keygen CPU cycle counts; also isolated forward/inverse NTT cycle counts
claimed_speedup: End-to-end vs pq-crystals reference C (Table 3): ML-KEM-512 decaps 1.32x, encaps 1.27x, keygen 1.17x (ML-KEM-768/1024 1.13-1.24x); ML-DSA-2 sign 1.26x, verify 1.16x, keygen 1.11x (ML-DSA-3/5 1.08-1.25x). NTT vs reference C: forward 1.47-1.83x, inverse 1.66-2.48x (Table 1). Vs formosa-mlkem Jasmin, ML-KEM NTT 1.26x and INTT 2.19x (round-trip 1.63x); these are kernel-level numbers, not end-to-end. Vs mlkem-native scalar C, the ML-KEM forward NTT is slower (0.86x) and INTT is 1.18x; vs mldsa-native, 1.66x/1.52x (Table 2).
compiler_and_flags: gcc-11.4 -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer (C, matching the pq-crystals test_speed setup); Jasmin 2025.6.1 + clang-14 -O3 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer -fwrapv (verified backend); 10k iterations, rdtsc with cpuid, median of three per-run medians
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2314 @ 2.80GHz, 4 cores, TurboBoost/Hyper-Threading disabled
tradeoffs: Improves only the NTT component, not a full drop-in library; targets ML-KEM/ML-DSA/FN-DSA jointly from one code generator, so gains are shared but modest end-to-end (<1.3x for most operations).
caveats: This is a 2026 ePrint preprint and not yet peer-reviewed. The code lives only at a double-blind-review anonymous.4open.science mirror (https://anonymous.4open.science/r/pkc_anonymous_artifact-8F22). Its web UI redirects, but its API serves the files. Links like this are temporary. All wins are over scalar reference C: no AVX2 backend is provided (the authors measured Plantard ~28% slower than Montgomery under AVX2), so this does not beat the optimized AVX2 ML-KEM/ML-DSA implementations, and the forward ML-KEM NTT loses to mlkem-native scalar C (0.86x). The Apache-2.0 license is from an anonymous copyright holder.

name: FN-DSA (Rust, Falcon-based post-quantum signatures)
workload: Single FN-DSA/512 (Falcon) key generation, signature generation and verification, measured in CPU clock cycles, compared in prose against OpenSSL's RSA-2048 signing/verification cost on the same CPU families
claimed_speedup: Prose only, no RSA numbers on page: on i5-8259U (x86_64) FN-DSA/512 is 'about as fast as RSA-2048 for verification, but about 2.5x faster for signature generation, and many times faster for key pair generation'; on the ARM Cortex-A76 'signature generation with this code is about 8 times faster than OpenSSL's RSA-2048'; FN-DSA/512 is said to be 'substantially faster than RSA-2048 on all these systems' except x86_64 verify parity. FN-DSA/512 cycles on i5-8259U: keygen 8.91M, sign 1.13M, verify 63.3K.
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.97.1 (rustc) for the i5-8259U table (toolchain for ARM/RISC-V tables not stated); cargo bench harness in fn-dsa/benches (keygen.rs, sign.rs, verify.rs) reading rdtsc / pmccntr_el0 / rdcycle; AVX2 path auto-selected at runtime on x86_64, NEON on aarch64; RUSTFLAGS/target-cpu not stated; OpenSSL build/version/flags for the RSA-2048 comparison not stated
hardware: Intel i5-8259U (Coffee Lake); ARM Cortex-A76 (Broadcom BCM2712C1); SiFive U74 (RISC-V)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust with runtime AVX2/NEON dispatch; a feature-parity C port exists (pornin/c-fn-dsa) with similar performance; Falcon/FN-DSA keys and signatures are larger than RSA/ECDSA equivalents and keygen is comparatively expensive (though far faster than RSA-2048 keygen); floating-point signing requires care for constant-time behavior
caveats: The OpenSSL RSA-2048 comparison is a prose claim ('about 8 times faster', 'about 2.5x') with no RSA cycle table, OpenSSL version or flags, and the repo's benches do not run OpenSSL, so it is a first-party claim with partial methodology, not a reproducible A/B benchmark. Per the README, no FN-DSA draft has been published yet and the 2026-07-22 update implements a 'best guess' at the upcoming draft; keys/signatures are expected to break compatibility before v1.0. Unlicense (public-domain dedication): no patent grant.

name: GOLF: GPU-accelerated Optimization for Lattice-based FALCON
baseline: Falcon reference implementation throughput as published on falcon-sign.info (Intel Core i5-8259U @ 2.3 GHz, TurboBoost off), cited as Fouque et al. (Ref) in Table II and not re-run by the authors; also prior CPU/GPU Falcon papers
workload: Batch Falcon signature generation and verification throughput (ops/s) on an RTX 4090 (and an A100), compared with the Falcon reference implementation's published single-machine CPU throughput and with prior CPU/GPU Falcon implementations (Table II)
claimed_speedup: Falcon on RTX 4090: 420.25 kops/s signing (Table II: 420,250.10 ops/s) and 10,311.04 kops/s verification. The '42.02 kops/s' in the ePrint web abstract is a typo; the PDF abstract and Table II both say 420.25. Against the reference Falcon figures from falcon-sign.info (i5-8259U) the gain is 70.65x signing / 369.13x verification (the paper's '70.65x to 369.13x', Sec. IV-E). The abstract's 58.05x/73.14x is actually against the fastest CPU implementation (Nguyen et al., Apple M1), as Sec. IV-E and the conclusion show. GOLF is also 7.17x/3.79x over the fastest prior GPU work (Lee et al., on an A100, so different hardware) and 2.69x/1.53x on the same A100.
compiler_and_flags: NVCC, CUDA 12.1, -rdc=true -arch sm_89 -maxrregcount=127 (GPU side); the reference baseline's compiler and flags are not stated (numbers copied from falcon-sign.info)
hardware: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 (24 GB) with an AMD Ryzen 7 5700G host; also tested on an NVIDIA A100. The reference baseline numbers come from the Falcon website on an Intel Core i5-8259U (the paper's text also says i5-8279U).
tradeoffs: No public code repository located; batched GPU throughput number, not single-operation latency; needs large batches and a CUDA GPU to realize the claimed gains.
caveats: Peer-reviewed as IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security vol. 20, pp. 9441-9453 (2025), doi:10.1109/TIFS.2025.3599681; the ePrint copy is labelled Preprint. The reference baseline was copied from the Falcon website (different CPU, flags unstated), not re-run. GPU batch throughput against a single CPU is a cross-hardware comparison, and the 7.17x/3.79x GPU comparison is also cross-hardware (RTX 4090 vs A100). The abstract labels 58.05x/73.14x as 'over the reference', but it is really against Nguyen et al. on an Apple M1. No code is linked from the paper. The repo github.com/russdrh/FP-GOLF (on the first author's account; a CUDA Falcon port with no license, created 2026-05, 0 stars) may be related but is not confirmed as the GOLF artifact, and its Makefile flags differ (sm_80, -use_fast_math).
found_via: IACR ePrint search "GPU signature verification throughput" -> eprint.iacr.org/2025/749

verification.tier_reason: The paper was peer-reviewed (IEEE TIFS 2025), but its reference-Falcon baseline figures (5,948.1 sign/s, 27,933.0 verify/s) were copied from falcon-sign.info (i5-8259U, compiler flags not given) rather than re-run. The GPU-vs-single-core-CPU gains are 70.65x/369.13x, over 50x with the baseline flags unstated, so the implausible-ratio rule caps the tier at C. No code is linked from the paper.
verification.notes: The headline signing figure in the record (42.02 kops/s) is a 10x typo on the ePrint landing page; the PDF says 420.25 kops/s. The 58.05x/73.14x ratios are against the Apple M1 implementation, not the reference; against the reference the gain is larger (70.65x/369.13x). I kept the tier at C because of the copied, flag-less baseline and the >50x ratio, even though the paper is peer-reviewed (TIFS). I did not treat the russdrh/FP-GOLF repo as the project's code.

name: GRASP: GPU-based paRallel Accelerated SPHINCS+
baseline: NIST PQC SPHINCS+ reference C code (version 3.0), SHA-256 simple fast parameter sets, run by the authors on a single core of an AMD Ryzen 5 5600G; also the open-source GPU SPHINCS+ of Kim et al. (re-run on the same GPU) plus prior GPU/FPGA works
workload: SPHINCS+-SHA256-128f/192f/256f-simple signing and verification throughput (ops/s) on an RTX 4090, compared with the NIST reference C code on one Ryzen 5 5600G core and with prior GPU/FPGA SPHINCS+ implementations; headline GPU numbers exclude host-device memcpy time
claimed_speedup: SPHINCS+-SHA256-f-simple on RTX 4090, kernel time only (memcpy excluded). Signing: 146,363 / 82,621 / 40,489 ops/s at levels 1/3/5, which is 3659.08x / 3177.73x / 3114.54x over the single-core NIST reference (40/26/13 ops/s). Verification: 1,499,590 / 933,696 / 886,362 ops/s, which is 2029.22x / 1897.76x / 1820.05x over the reference (Table VI). Against Kim et al. (open-source, re-run on the same RTX 4090): signing 1.37x/1.79x/1.58x (1.36x/1.65x/1.49x with memcpy) and verification 1.53x/1.80x/3.45x.
compiler_and_flags: NVCC on Linux (version and flags not stated); the CPU reference build's compiler and flags are not stated
hardware: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 (also RTX 3090 and GTX 1080); CPU baseline on an AMD Ryzen 5 5600G (single core); Linux
tradeoffs: No public code repository located; GPU batch throughput vs single-thread reference, not representative of single-signature latency; SPHINCS+ is already the slowest NIST signature scheme so large multiples over its reference implementation are expected.
caveats: Peer-reviewed as IEEE Transactions on Computers vol. 75, no. 4, pp. 1579-1592 (2026), doi:10.1109/TC.2026.3654650; the ePrint copy is labelled Preprint and has a different title ('GRASP: Accelerating Hash-based PQC Performance on GPU Parallel Architecture'). The >1000x figure is GPU batch throughput against a single CPU core, with compiler flags unstated on both sides. The headline GPU numbers exclude memcpy. The level-3 verification figure in the text (1,408,846 ops/s) conflicts with Table VI (933,696 ops/s). No code release was found.
found_via: IACR ePrint search "GPU signature verification throughput" -> eprint.iacr.org/2024/1030

verification.tier_reason: The paper was peer-reviewed (IEEE Transactions on Computers 2026) and re-ran the NIST SPHINCS+ reference C code v3.0 on one core of a Ryzen 5 5600G. However, neither the NVCC nor the CPU compiler flags/version are stated, and the gains are 1820x-3659x, so the implausible-ratio rule caps the tier at C. No code was released.
verification.notes: The record's claim matches the abstract. I added the concrete per-level numbers and the peer-reviewed venue (IEEE TC 2026). Tier stays C because of the >1000x cross-hardware ratio with unstated flags. The more meaningful result is 1.37x-3.45x against Kim et al.'s open-source GPU code, re-run on the same RTX 4090.

corrected_fields.baseline: SPHINCS+ NIST reference implementation (the portable C backend bundled in liboqs)
