name: ML-KEM AVX-512 optimization for TLS 1.3 (Zheng et al., Fudan University)
baseline: pq-crystals Kyber 'standard' branch AVX2 implementation (FIPS 203 draft code, the paper's ref [5]) for ML-KEM cycle counts; liboqs 0.10.1 ML-KEM AVX2 via OQS-provider on OpenSSL 3.3.0-dev for TLS 1.3 handshakes/sec
workload: ML-KEM-512/768/1024 key generation, encapsulation, and decapsulation, plus a batch key-generation variant, integrated into liboqs and OQS-provider for OpenSSL/TLS 1.3 handshakes
claimed_speedup: AVX-512 ML-KEM is 1.30x-1.64x faster than the AVX2 implementation in median CPU cycles (max 1.64x for ML-KEM-1024 Encaps: 25,062 vs 41,162 cycles). Batched keygen (8 keys) gives 4.9x / 4.2x / 3.5x for ML-KEM-512/768/1024 per the paper. TLS 1.3 handshake gains are small, about 0.4-5.6% more connections/sec in most PQ-only and hybrid configurations (derived from page data), and the paper itself calls them 'subtle' / 'minimal'.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 9.4.0 (optimization flags not stated); AVX-512 disabled when benchmarking the AVX2 baseline; Turbo Boost and hyper-threading left on; median of 100,000 runs; TLS tests with OpenSSL 3.3.0-dev + OQS provider (openssl s_server / s_time)
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8475B, 4 vCPUs, 8 GiB memory (Alibaba Cloud c8i compute-optimized instance, Sapphire Rapids)
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512; the paper's batch key-generation method requires protocol-level changes to how TLS 1.3 handshakes request/consume KEM keys, not just a drop-in library swap.
caveats: Published at ESORICS 2024 (LNCS), but the paper only says 'we will later open source our code' and no public repository was found (GitHub repo and code search), so has_code=false and the result cannot be reproduced. Table 3 has one cell where AVX-512 is slower (ML-KEM-1024/Dilithium5: 2451.08 vs 3191.46 conn/s, an AVX2 value that duplicates the Falcon512 cell, so possibly a copy error). The stated batch-keygen ratios are a little higher than the table implies against non-batched AVX-512 keygen (about 4.7x / 4.0x / 3.4x, derived from page data). Handshake gains are within about 6%.
found_via: arXiv search 'ML-KEM AVX' -> arXiv:2404.13544 'Faster Post-Quantum TLS 1.3 Based on ML-KEM: Implementation and Assessment'

verification.tier_reason: Upgraded C->B: the paper was peer-reviewed and published at ESORICS 2024 (LNCS, DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-70890-9_7, pp. 123-143), and its Table 2 shows 1.30-1.64x cycle-count wins over the pq-crystals Kyber AVX2 code (GCC 9.4.0, Xeon Platinum 8475B). It falls short of A because no code has been released (searched GitHub) and compiler flags are not stated.
verification.notes: Hardware and compiler claims check out; the baseline for the headline 1.64x is the pq-crystals standard-branch AVX2 code, not liboqs itself (liboqs 0.10.1 is only the integration target), so I corrected baseline to say so and left baseline_in_list=true because the TLS comparison runs through liboqs. The tier is upgraded to B on the confirmed ESORICS 2024 publication.

corrected_fields.baseline: liboqs ML-KEM AVX2 implementation (liboqs 0.10.1)
corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Up to 1.64x speedup over the latest AVX2 implementation for core ML-KEM operations; batch key generation is 3.5x-4.9x faster; results in more TLS 1.3 handshakes/sec in both PQ-only and hybrid modes
corrected_fields.caveats: Paper explicitly states 'we will later open source our code' and no matching public repository could be found this session, so has_code=false and tier capped at C despite compiler/CPU/OpenSSL-version being stated; peer-review venue for this arXiv preprint is unconfirmed.

name: Snowshoe (catid/snowshoe)
workload: Elliptic-curve scalar multiplication / EC-DH and signature-style operations (ec_mul, ec_simul) on a custom ~252-bit curve at ~128-bit security, cycle-counted with RDTSC (Turbo Boost disabled), compared against OpenSSL 1.0.1e's P-256 timing tests and a third-party paper's OpenSSL-optimization results
claimed_speedup: README: 'Kasper demonstrates that the improvements in the paper are roughly 3x faster than normal OpenSSL, pegging Snowshoe roughly 6x faster than OpenSSL 1.0.1e for the same security level' (an indirect estimate). It also says the author's own OpenSSL 1.0.1e `make tests` run (64-bit, ectest.c timing macros enabled) showed 'roughly 100 usec to generate a key (4x slower)' and 'roughly 400 usec for EC-DH (8x slower)'. Both ratios are stated verbatim on the page, not derived. The same page says Crypto++ 5.6.2 and LibTomCrypt 1.17 ECC-256 are 'roughly 20x slower than Snowshoe'.
compiler_and_flags: Snowshoe side: Makefile default clang++ -m64 with OPTFLAGS -O4 (make ecmultest / make release); a GCC alternative, -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer -funroll-loops, is commented out. OpenSSL 1.0.1e side: default 64-bit build, flags unstated.
hardware: Snowshoe's own RDTSC runs, Turbo Boost off: Core i5-2557M (MacBook Air), Core i5-2500S (iMac) and Core i7 620M (Windows 7 laptop). The page does not say which machine ran OpenSSL 1.0.1e. The i7-2600 and i7-3770 figures on the page are Longa's implementation numbers, not Snowshoe-vs-OpenSSL.
tradeoffs: Targets a custom non-standard curve rather than NIST P-256 or secp256k1, limiting interoperability; project is explicitly pre-1.0/experimental
caveats: The OpenSSL 1.0.1e baseline (2013) is over a decade old. The '6x' figure is an indirect estimate that chains Kasper's paper (about 3x over stock OpenSSL on Core 2) with the author's projected Snowshoe cycle counts. The 4x/8x figures come from the author's own rough OpenSSL run ('roughly' 100/400 usec) on an unstated machine, with no harness in the repo. On the same page some competing 128-bit curve implementations beat Snowshoe on some operations: Longa ecmul_gen/ecmul/ecsimul_gen, Kummer ecmul 72kcy, kumfp127g ecmul and Hamburg ecmul_gen per the page's labels. The BSD-3-Clause LICENSE was added only in 2018 (PR #3). Custom non-standard curve.
found_via: gh search code "x faster" "signature verification" -> catid/snowshoe README Benchmarks section

verification.tier_reason: The README's Comparisons section compares Snowshoe with OpenSSL 1.0.1e (ecp_nistp256.c). It gives an indirect '~6x faster' estimate built on Kasper's paper, plus the author's own approximate OpenSSL `make tests` timings ('roughly 100 usec' keygen, 4x slower; 'roughly 400 usec' EC-DH, 8x slower). The Snowshoe side has public bench code (tests/ecmul_test.cpp, tests/snowshoe_test.cpp, Makefile clang++ -m64 -O4, median of 10,000 RDTSC runs, CPUs named). The OpenSSL run gives no machine or flags and ships no harness, so this is first-party partial methodology: C.
verification.notes: Real entry, accurate apart from a mislabel: the 4x/8x ratios were marked '(derived from page data)' but the README states them outright. The hardware field wrongly mixed in Longa's CPUs. Metadata checked: BSD-3-Clause, not archived, not a fork, 64 stars, last commit 2018-02-03, so abandoned is correct.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: author states Snowshoe is 'roughly 6x faster than OpenSSL 1.0.1e for the same security level'; own OpenSSL 1.0.1e make-tests run showed ~4x slower key generation and ~8x slower EC-DH than Snowshoe (derived from page data)
corrected_fields.hardware: Sandy Bridge / Ivy Bridge era Intel CPUs (Core i5-2557M, i7-2600, i7-3770), Turbo Boost disabled, RDTSC cycle counts
corrected_fields.caveats: OpenSSL baseline (1.0.1e, 2013) is over a decade out of date; the 6x figure combines the author's own cycle counts with a separate paper's (Kasper) OpenSSL optimization results via derived arithmetic rather than a single direct head-to-head run; capped at tier C for outdated/indirect baseline per hard rules

name: watsign
workload: Ed25519 sign and verify of short and long messages, warm (50x average after 50x warmup) and cold-start timings, in-browser via puppeteer
claimed_speedup: 4-6x faster than tweetnacl-js warmed up, up to 33x faster on cold start after page load; 1.2-3x faster than noble-ed25519 warmed up, up to 17x on cold start
hardware: Intel i7-10700, Chromium 93 (via puppeteer)
tradeoffs: JS/WebAssembly only, not usable directly from C++; ports the TweetNaCl algorithm rather than a novel design; API is async-only because of WebAssembly plus native SHA-512; signing/verification only, no encryption support.
caveats: First-party benchmark from the project's own repo. The harness is test/performance.js, which runs test/test-watsign.js, test/test-tweetnacl-js.js and test/test-noble-ed25519.js via chrode (headless Chromium), with timing in test/perf.js. The Performance section dates from October 2021 (commit 'cleaner perf test, add comparison with noble-ed25519', 2021-10-06) on Chromium 93 and has not been revalidated on modern V8 or hardware. The 'up to 33x' figure comes from a single cold-start sample (sign long msg: 43.88 ms vs 1.32 ms), and the README says cold-start runs vary between runs. The steady-state figure is 4-6x (derived from page data: 4.3x sign short, 5.1x verify short, 5.9x sign long, 5.6x verify long). Against noble-ed25519, page data gives 1.3-2.8x warm, which the README rounds to 1.2-3x. Last commit 2024-04-15 (v0.1.9), about 2.4 years before today.
found_via: Hacker News: search query "faster Ed25519" surfaced "Tweetnacl's ed25519 signatures, ported to WebAssembly, 5x faster" (2021-12-22)

verification.tier_reason: The README Performance section gives first-party timings against tweetnacl-js and noble-ed25519 on an Intel i7-10700 in Chromium 93. The harness is public (test/performance.js runs test-watsign.js, test-tweetnacl-js.js and test-noble-ed25519.js through chrode, with timing in test/perf.js), but there are no engine flags or build settings, so this is C, not A.
verification.notes: The claims match the README exactly and the ratios check out against the listed timings. The only real fix is the benchmark script path: the record's caveats pointed to src-experiments/test/, but the scripts live in test/. Metadata confirmed: MIT, not a fork, not archived, 14 stars, last commit 2024-04-15, so stale is correct.

corrected_fields.caveats: First-party benchmark on the project's own repo (comparison scripts present: src-experiments/test/perf.js, performance.js, test-tweetnacl-js.js, test-noble-ed25519.js, test-watsign.js); numbers are from 2021 on Chromium 93 and have not been revalidated on modern engines/hardware; the 'up to 33x' figure is a cold-start outlier versus the more representative 4-6x warm-run figure; last commit 2024-04-15, over two years stale as of today.
